items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Washington County, PA
items.meta: Own minerals in Washington County? We buy Marcellus and Utica interests directly, explain your division order in plain English, and close on your timeline.

sections.html:
The owner's grandfather signed his first gas lease in Washington County back when a well was just a curiosity on the back forty. Now it's the wettest, busiest part of the whole Marcellus play, and the mail still shows up confusing.

Washington County sits at the center of the Marcellus wet-gas window, and it has for over a decade. Range Resources drilled some of its earliest Pennsylvania pads here, and EQT, CNX, and a handful of smaller operators followed. If your family holds minerals anywhere between Canonsburg and California, Claysville and Charleroi, there's a decent chance a horizontal well has already crossed under your ground, or a unit line has swept through it, whether a rig ever sat on your own surface or not.

That density is exactly why Washington County owners end up with some of the most confusing royalty statements in the state. Pooled units, allocation wells, deducted post-production costs, an interest that got split four ways in a will from 1987 and never got cleaned up at the recorder of deeds. We've bought minerals across this county for years, and we still see a new statement every week that would take a landman a full afternoon to untangle.

sections.title: Why Washington County Draws So Much Drilling Interest
sections.html:
Washington County isn't a fringe county in the Marcellus play, it's close to the heart of it. The rock here runs thick and rich in natural gas liquids, which is why operators pay more attention to a lease here than they do thirty miles north where the gas turns dry. Ethane and propane content in the wet-gas window means a well here can be worth drilling even when Henry Hub prices sag, because the liquids carry their own separate value.

That's part of why lease and unit activity never fully stopped here the way it did in some drier counties during the 2015-2016 downturn. Companies kept permitting, kept pooling new units, kept coming back for infill wells on pads that had already produced for years. If you inherited an interest here, odds are good it's tied to a unit that's actually active, not sitting dormant waiting on a pipeline that may never come.

sections.title: The Post-Production Deduction Fight Owners Are Still Fighting
sections.html:
Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a floor of one-eighth, but it doesn't say a word about what an operator can deduct before that eighth ever gets calculated. Gathering, compression, dehydration, transportation to the sale point, marketing fees, they all get taken off the top on a lot of older Washington County leases, and the Kilmer v. Elexco decision from the state Supreme Court gave operators room to do exactly that as long as the lease language allows it. We've had sellers hand us a royalty statement showing a gross value on one line and a net check for barely half of it, and the confusion on their face is the same look the owner's own family had the first time it happened to us.

If your lease was signed before anyone in your family thought to ask a landman about a no-deduction clause, you're probably living with that math every month. It's one of the biggest reasons owners here decide to sell rather than keep watching costs eat into a check that should be bigger.

sections.title: Act 13 Impact Fees and What They Actually Mean for You
sections.html: Act 13 set up an impact fee system in 2012 that sends unconventional well fees to counties and municipalities, and Washington County has collected some of the largest impact fee distributions in the Commonwealth because it hosts so many producing wells. That money pays for roads, emergency services, and local infrastructure, but it's a fee paid by the operator to local government, not a royalty paid to you as the mineral owner. We mention it because a lot of owners hear impact fee on county budget news and assume it has something to do with their own check. It doesn't, and understanding that distinction helps you read your own statement more clearly instead of chasing numbers that were never yours to begin with.

sections.title: How a Sale Works if You Own Minerals Here
sections.html: We start with your deed and your most recent division order, run the parcel against active units and permits filed with the Pennsylvania DEP, and give you a straightforward cash offer based on what's actually producing or reasonably likely to be developed. There's no pressure to sign fast and no vague promise of a number we can't back up. Some families sell everything, others keep a piece and sell the rest to cover a specific need. We close through a title company, the same way any real estate transaction in Washington County closes, and we handle the recorder of deeds paperwork ourselves.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Washington County minerals are held by production?
faqs.a: Check your lease's habendum clause and compare it against permits and unit filings on the DEP's oil and gas mapping tool. If a well within your unit has been producing, most standard leases stay held by production indefinitely. We can walk you through this at no cost before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests that aren't currently leased?
faqs.a: Yes. Unleased minerals in an active area like Washington County still carry value because a future operator will eventually need to lease or pool them. The value is different than a producing, leased interest, but it's rarely zero.

faqs.q: Will selling affect the impact fee money the county collects?
faqs.a: No. Act 13 impact fees are paid by the operator based on the well, not tied to who owns the mineral interest underneath it. Selling your minerals has no effect on county or municipal impact fee revenue.

faqs.q: What if your deed only covers a fractional interest?
faqs.a: That's common in Washington County, especially on land that's passed through several generations. We buy fractional and undivided interests regularly and can explain exactly how your percentage translates to value.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: It isn't required, but for larger or more complicated interests we always encourage owners to have their own attorney review the purchase agreement. We're happy to work alongside whoever you choose.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Greene County, PA
items.meta: Greene County sits in the richest part of PA's Marcellus wet-gas fairway. We buy mineral and royalty interests around Waynesburg — honest numbers, no pressure.

sections.html:
Greene County has some of the best Marcellus rock in the state, and mineral owners here know it — which is exactly why so many of them are frustrated with what actually lands in the mailbox.

Greene County is where the Marcellus wet-gas window runs deepest and richest in Pennsylvania, and EQT has drilled it hard for well over a decade. Families around Waynesburg, Greensboro, and the smaller townships toward the West Virginia line often have a wall of royalty statements going back years — and just as often, a growing list of questions about why the number on line one keeps shrinking by the time it reaches the net-paid column.

We buy mineral and royalty interests throughout Greene County, whether you're holding producing acreage under an active EQT unit, a fractional interest split among heirs from a family farm, or ground that's leased but not yet drilled. If the coal-mining history of this county is also tangled up in your deed, we've seen that plenty of times too and know what to look for.

sections.title: The deepest, richest corner of the Marcellus fairway
sections.html:
Greene County sits at the heart of the wet-gas Marcellus core, where the shale is thick, deep, and liquids-rich compared to counties further north. That's part of why operators have run some of the longest laterals and highest-producing units in the state through here, and why decline curves on Greene County wells tend to hold up better in the early years than in thinner, shallower parts of the play.

It also means spacing units in Greene County can pull in a lot of small tracts under one pooled unit, so it's common for a single family's acreage to represent a modest slice of a much bigger drilling unit rather than a standalone lease.

sections.title: Coal country first, gas country second
sections.html:
Long before Marcellus, Greene County was — and still is — deep coal country, home to some of the largest underground longwall mines in the eastern United States. That history left its mark on title records the same way it did in Fayette County: coal, oil, and gas were frequently severed into separate ownership generations ago, and Waynesburg's Recorder of Deeds office holds decades of those old severance instruments.

If your family has farmed or held land here for multiple generations, there's a real chance the surface, the coal, and the oil and gas rights are no longer all in the same hands — worth confirming before you assume you know exactly what you're selling.

sections.title: Why the royalty check never matches the lease percentage
sections.html:
The single most common call we get from Greene County owners is some version of 'the owner's lease says an eighth, so why is the owner's check smaller than that.' The answer is almost always post-production deductions — gathering, compression, dehydration, and marketing charges the operator nets out before paying royalty, depending on how the lease was written. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a statutory 1/8 floor on the gross royalty owed, but the Kilmer v. Elexco decision left the door open for deductions to still apply on top of that floor in a lot of lease language.

Act 13 impact fees are a different, unrelated stream of money that Greene County and its municipalities receive per well for roads, water systems, and emergency services — it doesn't flow to individual royalty owners, so it never shows up on a royalty statement no matter how much local infrastructure it funds.

sections.title: What drives value on Greene County acreage
sections.html:
Because this is such an active part of the play, well performance history matters more here than almost anywhere else in the state — a tract under a strong-producing EQT unit prices very differently than acreage that's leased but sitting in a queue for future development. Remaining primary term, pooling and unitization language, and whether your interest is producing, non-producing-but-leased, or open all factor in.

We won't quote a number sight unseen. Send us what you have — a lease, a division order, a recent royalty statement, or even just the well name if you know it — and we'll tell you plainly what we can offer and why.

faqs.q: Why is Greene County considered such a strong part of the Marcellus play?
faqs.a: It sits in the deepest, most liquids-rich part of the wet-gas fairway, which generally supports stronger well performance than thinner or shallower parts of the formation. That's a general characteristic of the play here, not a promise about what any specific well or tract will produce.

faqs.q: Your family's Greene County land has old coal leases too — does that affect an oil and gas sale?
faqs.a: It can affect the title work, since coal, oil, and gas were often severed separately in this county's deeds. It doesn't usually stop an oil and gas sale, but we do want to see the relevant documents so we understand exactly what interest is being conveyed.

faqs.q: Are Act 13 impact fees paid to mineral owners in Greene County?
faqs.a: No. Impact fees are paid by operators per well to the state, then distributed to counties and municipalities for infrastructure and services. They're a public-fund mechanism, not a payment to individual royalty owners, so they won't appear on your check.

faqs.q: What's a pooled or unitized interest and why does your Greene County lease mention it?
faqs.a: Pooling combines multiple owners' tracts into one drilling unit so a single horizontal well can be produced across all of them, with each owner paid their proportionate share. It's standard in this part of the Marcellus play given how large modern units have become, and it directly affects how your royalty interest is valued.

faqs.q: Do you buy both producing and non-producing mineral interests in Greene County?
faqs.a: Yes, we look at producing royalty interests, leased-but-undrilled acreage, and in some cases unleased minerals. What we can offer depends on the specifics, but we're happy to review any of these.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Susquehanna County, PA
items.meta: We buy dry-gas Marcellus mineral interests in Susquehanna County, explain your royalty statement honestly, and pay cash without dragging you into a bidding war.

sections.html:
Susquehanna County was one of the very first places in Pennsylvania where a landman knocked on a farmhouse door and changed a family's finances overnight. Fifteen years later, a lot of those same families still don't fully trust the check that shows up.

Long before Washington County or Greene County saw a Marcellus rig, Susquehanna County was already leased up. Cabot Oil & Gas, now Coterra, built one of the largest and most productive positions in the entire play here, and the county's dry-gas wells are still some of the most efficient producers in the Commonwealth. Montrose is the county seat, and the recorder of deeds office there has spent the better part of two decades processing lease assignments, division orders, and probate filings tied to gas.

That early start cuts both ways for the families who own minerals here now. On one hand, these are some of the longest-producing, best-understood wells in the Marcellus. On the other, a lot of the original leases were signed in 2008 and 2009, before landowners in this part of the state had much leverage or much legal advice, and those older lease terms are exactly the ones causing the most grief on today's royalty statements.

sections.title: Dry Gas, Long Laterals, and Decades of Production History
sections.html:
Susquehanna County sits in the dry-gas core of the Marcellus, meaning the gas here is almost pure methane with little of the natural gas liquids you'd find further south and west. Operators compensate with scale: some of the longest laterals and largest pad developments in the state have been drilled here, and a single unit can span multiple family tracts. If you own a fractional interest in a Susquehanna County unit, it may be tied to a well that's been producing steadily for well over a decade, which gives us a strong production history to value your interest against rather than guessing at what a brand-new well might do.

That long track record is actually an advantage when you're deciding whether to sell. We can look at years of actual volumes instead of a projection, and that makes for a fairer, better-grounded offer.

sections.title: Why So Many Early Leases Left Owners Exposed
sections.html:
A lot of the original Susquehanna County leases were signed at a pace that outran the legal advice available at the time. Post-production cost deduction language, in particular, was often boilerplate that favored the operator, and after the Kilmer v. Elexco ruling gave that language real teeth, owners here started seeing gathering, compression, and marketing fees carved out of their royalty before the one-eighth minimum required under Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act was ever calculated. We've reviewed statements from Susquehanna County families where the net check came in at little more than half the gross value of the gas.

It's not fraud, it's contract language most people signed without a landman or attorney explaining what it would mean fifteen years down the road. We don't judge anyone for that. We ask the same questions our own family had to learn to ask.

sections.title: Act 13 Impact Fees in a County Built on Gas Revenue
sections.html: Susquehanna County has depended on Act 13 impact fee distributions since the law passed in 2012, using the money for roads, emergency services, and local infrastructure that a rural county budget couldn't otherwise carry. That fee is paid by the well operator to the county and its municipalities, though, not to you as a mineral owner, and it has nothing to do with what shows up on your own royalty statement. Understanding that separation matters here more than almost anywhere else in the state, because Susquehanna County residents hear about impact fee money constantly and it's easy to conflate it with personal royalty income.

sections.title: What Selling Looks Like for a Susquehanna County Owner
sections.html: Because so many wells here have a long production history, we can often put together an offer faster than in newer counties. We pull your deed, confirm your interest against the unit and any pooling order on file, review recent statements if you have them, and give you a number based on real production, not a guess. Some owners sell a full interest, others carve out and sell a term interest while keeping the rest in the family. We close through a title company and record everything properly at the courthouse in Montrose.

faqs.q: Is Susquehanna County still an active drilling area?
faqs.a: Yes, though the pace has slowed from the peak years. Existing wells continue producing, and infill development and refracturing still happen on established pads, which keeps many older units active.

faqs.q: Your original lease was signed in 2008. Does it still apply?
faqs.a: Most Marcellus leases from that era include a habendum clause that keeps the lease in force as long as the well is held by production, so yes, it likely still governs your interest even today.

faqs.q: Why is your royalty check so much smaller than you expected from the gross gas value?
faqs.a: Post-production cost deductions, gathering, compression, dehydration, and marketing fees, are the most common reason. Pennsylvania's minimum royalty law guarantees one-eighth of the gross before most of those deductions, but many older leases allow deductions after that calculation.

faqs.q: Does the county impact fee affect your royalty payment?
faqs.a: No. Act 13 impact fees go to county and municipal government from the well operator directly and have no bearing on the royalty calculation in your lease or division order.

faqs.q: Can you buy an interest you inherited that was never formally transferred?
faqs.a: Often, yes, though we'll need to help you clear title through probate or an affidavit of heirship first. We can walk you through exactly what the recorder of deeds office in Montrose will require.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Bradford County, PA
items.meta: Bradford County mineral owners: understand your dry-gas Marcellus royalty, deductions, and Act 13 fees, then get a fair cash offer.

sections.html:
Bradford County was ground zero for the northeastern Marcellus rush, and nearly two decades later, a lot of the families who signed those first leases still don't fully understand what's driving their royalty check.

When Chesapeake Energy and other operators moved into northeastern Pennsylvania in the mid-2000s, Bradford County was where the leasing pressure hit hardest and fastest. Landmen worked the county township by township, farm by farm, and within a few years a huge share of the county's private mineral acreage was under lease. Towanda, the county seat, became a hub for that early industry activity, and towns across the county, Athens, Canton, Burlington, Alba, and dozens of smaller communities, all became part of one of the most intensely developed dry-gas fields in the country.

We've held minerals through leasing rushes and slow declines ourselves, and we know how disorienting it can be to hold an interest for almost twenty years and still feel like nobody's ever really explained what it's worth or why the check looks the way it does. That's what we try to fix before we ever discuss a number with you.

sections.title: The dry-gas core of the northeastern Marcellus play
sections.html:
Bradford County sits over some of the thickest, most productive dry-gas Marcellus shale anywhere in Pennsylvania, which is exactly why operators pursued leasehold here so aggressively in the early boom years. Unlike the wet-gas counties of southwestern Pennsylvania, most Bradford County production carries little to no natural gas liquids content, meaning the post-production deduction structure on a typical royalty statement here is generally simpler, limited mostly to gathering, compression, and transportation costs rather than liquids fractionation.

That doesn't mean deductions are small or easy to overlook. Under Pennsylvania's Kilmer v. Elexco decision, operators can still net these costs against your royalty even when your lease describes a share of gross proceeds, and for owners who signed leases before that ruling reshaped how the industry approached deductions statewide, the gap between expected and actual royalty income has been a real source of frustration for years.

sections.title: Nearly two decades of production history
sections.html:
Because so much of Bradford County's Marcellus leasing happened early, in the mid-to-late 2000s, most producing wells here are now well past their steepest decline years and settled into a longer, more predictable production tail. That maturity is actually an advantage for valuing your interest accurately: we're working from real, multi-year data rather than a projection based on a new well's early performance.

For owners whose royalty checks have shrunk noticeably compared to what they were a decade ago, that's typically normal well decline rather than a sign of a problem, though it's still worth reviewing your specific statement to be sure nothing else is going on.

sections.title: The New York border and why this county leased so fast
sections.html: Bradford County's northern boundary runs along New York State, which has maintained a ban on high-volume hydraulic fracturing for years. That regulatory divide made Pennsylvania's side of the border, including Bradford County, an especially urgent target for operators trying to secure leasehold before landowners had a chance to see how the industry might develop, or not develop, just a few miles north.

sections.title: Act 13 impact fees across the county
sections.html: Given its high well count, Bradford County collects substantial Act 13 impact fee revenue each year, distributed to the county and its municipalities to help offset road wear, emergency services, and environmental costs tied to drilling activity. That revenue is separate from, and doesn't reduce, the post-production deductions taken from individual royalty checks, a distinction that surprises a lot of owners once they understand how the two systems work independently of each other.

sections.title: Confirming a nearly twenty-year-old chain of title
sections.html: We trace ownership through the Bradford County Recorder of Deeds, working back through however many transfers and generations it takes to confirm a clean, current picture, particularly important for owners whose interest has passed through an estate one or more times since the original lease was signed.

sections.title: Deciding whether to sell a legacy Marcellus interest
sections.html: For owners who've held minerals here since the early leasing rush and watched royalty income shrink year over year as wells mature, selling converts an uncertain, declining future income stream into one known number today. Others prefer to keep holding as long as production continues. We'll explain your specific situation clearly and let you decide with no pressure either way.

faqs.q: Why did Bradford County lease so much faster than other Pennsylvania counties?
faqs.a: Its position over thick, productive dry-gas Marcellus shale, combined with proximity to New York's fracking ban, made it an especially urgent target for operators during the early leasing rush.

faqs.q: Are dry-gas royalty deductions smaller than wet-gas ones?
faqs.a: Generally, yes, since there's no natural gas liquids processing step, though gathering, compression, and transportation deductions still apply under current Pennsylvania law.

faqs.q: Your well has been producing for close to twenty years. Is it still valuable?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A long production history gives us reliable data to value your interest confidently, which can make a mature well easier to price accurately than a new one.

faqs.q: Does Act 13 impact fee money reduce your royalty deductions?
faqs.a: No. The impact fee is a separate payment from the operator to the county and municipalities; it has no effect on the post-production deductions calculated against your personal royalty.

faqs.q: What if your interest has passed through more than one estate since the original lease?
faqs.a: That's common after nearly twenty years. We trace the full chain of title through the county recorder's office to confirm current ownership before making an offer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Butler County, PA
items.meta: Butler County mineral owners: understand your legacy oil and Marcellus rights, royalty deductions, and how to get a fair cash offer.

sections.html:
Butler County has been producing oil and gas since the 1870s, longer than almost anywhere else in the country, and that long history is exactly why so many families here hold mineral rights they've never had properly explained.

Butler is where Pennsylvania's oil story runs the deepest, not literally, since most of the county's original wells were shallow by today's standards, but historically. In the decades after the Drake Well came in near Titusville in 1859, the boom spread across the region, and Butler County became one of the state's major producing areas, with small fields, company towns, and thousands of shallow wells drilled across family farms. Some of those legacy wells are still marginally producing today, still generating a small royalty for descendants of the families who signed the original leases more than a century ago.

More recently, Marcellus development has reached significant parts of the county, adding a modern, deeper layer of leasing and production on top of that older conventional history. For a lot of Butler County families, that means untangling two very different eras of oil and gas paperwork before anyone can say with confidence what a mineral interest here is actually worth.

We've sold our own family's minerals before, and we know how disorienting it is to hold a deed that references formations, leases, and companies from different decades all at once. That's the exact confusion we specialize in clearing up before we ever put a number in front of you.

sections.title: From the county seat to the townships: where drilling happened
sections.html:
Butler, the county seat, anchors a county where legacy conventional oil and gas activity spread widely across the surrounding townships during the boom years of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Towns and small communities across the county, including places like Bruin, named directly for one of the era's oil fields, and Callery, carry that history in their local deed records.

Marcellus and, in places, deeper Utica development has since reached parts of Butler County as well, though less intensively than the core counties further southwest like Washington and Greene. A given family tract may hold rights to both the shallow legacy formations and the deeper unconventional zones, potentially under entirely separate leases negotiated decades apart.

sections.title: Coal severances and layered ownership
sections.html: Like much of southwestern Pennsylvania, Butler County land was often subject to coal severances that split the coal seam away from the rest of the mineral estate, sometimes leaving the oil and gas rights fully intact with the original family even when the surface and coal changed hands. Confirming exactly what survived a given coal-era transaction requires tracing the specific deed language, not assuming a standard outcome applies to every tract.

sections.title: The post-production deduction fight, statewide and here
sections.html:
Whether your Butler County interest is tied to a legacy conventional well or a modern Marcellus unit, Pennsylvania's Kilmer v. Elexco decision permits operators to deduct post-production costs, gathering, compression, processing, transportation, from your royalty before it's paid, even when your lease describes gross proceeds. It's one of the most consistent sources of frustration we hear from owners across this state, and Butler County is no exception.

The Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a legal floor of one-eighth of gross value as your royalty share under Pennsylvania law, a protection worth knowing about, though it doesn't prevent post-production deductions from reducing the net amount you actually receive.

sections.title: Act 13 impact fees in Butler County
sections.html: Unconventional wells drilled in Butler County generate Act 13 impact fee revenue, distributed to the county and its municipalities to help fund road maintenance, emergency services, and environmental programs affected by drilling activity. That fee is paid directly by the operator to the state and doesn't come out of your royalty, though it's often the first thing owners ask about once they understand how the deduction system on their own check works differently.

sections.title: What clean title looks like in this county
sections.html: Before any sale can close, your chain of title has to be traceable through the Butler County Recorder of Deeds back to a clean point of origin, whether that's a modern Marcellus lease or a shallow well drilled by your great-great-grandfather's generation. We do that title work ourselves, checking for old severances, unreleased leases, and any estate gaps that need to be resolved.

sections.title: Deciding whether to sell
sections.html: Some Butler County owners hold a legacy interest generating a small but steady check from a well that's been producing for a century; others hold a newer Marcellus interest still working through its decline curve. Whichever situation applies to you, we'll explain what drives your specific royalty and let you decide, with no pressure, whether converting it into a lump sum makes more sense than continuing to hold.

faqs.q: Is Butler County's oil history really that much older than Marcellus?
faqs.a: Yes. Commercial oil production in this part of Pennsylvania dates back to the 1870s and 1880s, roughly 130 years before Marcellus horizontal drilling arrived in the county.

faqs.q: Are old, shallow Butler County wells still worth anything?
faqs.a: Some are still marginally producing and generate a small royalty. We check the actual production status of any well tied to your interest before evaluating.

faqs.q: How does the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act protect you?
faqs.a: It sets a legal floor of one-eighth of gross value as your royalty rate under Pennsylvania law, though it doesn't prevent post-production deductions from reducing your net check.

faqs.q: Does the county's Act 13 impact fee revenue offset your personal royalty deductions?
faqs.a: No, they're entirely separate systems. The impact fee funds county and municipal programs; your royalty deductions are calculated independently under your specific lease.

faqs.q: What documents should you gather before contacting a buyer?
faqs.a: Any deed, lease, or recent royalty statement you have. If you're missing documents, we can typically locate what's needed through the Butler County Recorder of Deeds.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Westmoreland County, PA
items.meta: Own minerals in Westmoreland County, PA? We buy Marcellus interests directly from Greensburg to the river towns, with a real title review first.

sections.html:
Westmoreland County stretches from the Pittsburgh suburbs to the Laurel Highlands, and underneath a good part of it runs Marcellus shale that's been leased and drilled for close to two decades now.

Our family didn't sell minerals in Westmoreland County, our story runs through a different part of the state, but we've sat with enough families here to know the shape of it by heart. A farm gets leased sometime in the 2000s. A well gets drilled a few years later, sometimes on a shared multi-well pad with neighbors' tracts pooled in. Royalty checks start arriving, strong at first, then smaller, and smaller again, year after year, without anyone from the company ever explaining exactly why.

That's the gap we exist to close. We buy mineral and royalty interests directly from owners across Westmoreland County, and before we ever talk numbers, we make sure you understand what you actually own and what's actually being deducted from what you're paid.

sections.title: Coal Country First, Then Gas Country
sections.html:
Westmoreland County has one of the longest mineral extraction histories in Pennsylvania, going back to coal mining in the 1800s, long before anyone talked about the Marcellus. That layered history means a lot of tracts here had their coal rights severed from the surface generations before oil and gas leasing ever started, and sometimes the oil and gas rights were severed separately as well.

The result is that a single piece of Westmoreland County land can have three or four different owners across surface, coal, and oil and gas, each with their own deed history. Before we make an offer on any interest here, we confirm exactly which estate you hold and trace it back through the recorder of deeds in Greensburg, because getting that wrong helps nobody and can genuinely delay or derail a closing.

sections.title: Where the County Sits in the Marcellus Play
sections.html:
Westmoreland's Marcellus activity has generally been steadier and less explosive than the wet-gas core counties further southwest, like Washington and Greene. Its southern and western portions, closer to that fairway, tend to see richer liquids content and stronger historical leasing activity, while the northern half has seen more moderate development tied into shared multi-well pads.

Operators including CNX and EQT have both been active in the county over the years, developing units that pool multiple family tracts together. What that means practically is that two neighboring properties can have very different production histories depending on which unit and which pad they're tied to, so we always evaluate the specific unit behind your interest rather than assuming a county-wide number applies to you.

sections.title: The Deduction Problem Playing Out on Westmoreland Statements
sections.html:
Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act requires a lease to pay at least one-eighth net, and the Kilmer v. Elexco decision confirmed operators can deduct reasonable post-production costs, gathering, compression, dehydration, marketing, before calculating that net figure. Those two rules together mean a check can shrink year over year even while production stays relatively steady, as long as it stays above the statutory floor.

We've read enough of these statements across the county to recognize the pattern immediately: strong first-year payments, then a slow, steady erosion that looks confusing until someone actually walks you through where each deduction line is coming from. If your Westmoreland County royalty checks have been sliding and nobody's explained why, that's usually the answer, not a production problem, a deduction problem written right into the lease you signed years ago.

sections.title: Act 13 Impact Fees Fund the County, Not Your Check
sections.html:
Westmoreland County collects Act 13 impact fee revenue on unconventional wells drilled here, money that goes toward road repair, emergency services, and environmental programs at the county and municipal level. It's a meaningful source of local funding, but it's entirely separate from your royalty and doesn't flow to individual mineral owners.

We mention this because it comes up often enough in conversations with owners who assume some portion of that county revenue is somehow tied to their personal payments. It isn't, and understanding that distinction helps clarify what actually drives the value of your interest: your lease terms and your unit's production, not county-level fee programs.

sections.title: Handling Heirs, Fractional Interests, and Old Deeds
sections.html:
A large share of the mineral interests we review in Westmoreland County were never purchased outright by the current owner, they were inherited, often split among several siblings or cousins after a parent or grandparent passed. That kind of fractional ownership is common across the county's older farm and coal-town families, and it doesn't need to be a barrier to selling.

We can work with individual heirs directly, buying just your share without requiring every co-owner to participate, or coordinate a single closing that pays each family member according to their confirmed interest. Either way, we do the courthouse work to confirm exactly what each person owns before any paperwork gets signed.

faqs.q: What areas of Westmoreland County have the most Marcellus activity?
faqs.a: The southern and western portions of the county, closer to the Washington and Fayette county lines, tend to sit nearer the wet gas fairway and have seen stronger historical leasing and drilling activity than the northern half.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own oil and gas rights or coal rights?
faqs.a: Your deed and any historical severance documents will specify which estate you hold. We trace this through the Westmoreland County recorder of deeds as part of every review, at no cost to you.

faqs.q: Why has your royalty check shrunk even though production seems steady?
faqs.a: Pennsylvania law generally allows operators to deduct reasonable post-production costs, gathering, compression, marketing, as long as your payment stays above the one-eighth net floor. That deduction language is often the reason for a declining check, not a change in the well itself.

faqs.q: Does the Act 13 impact fee pay mineral owners directly?
faqs.a: No. Impact fee revenue funds county and municipal infrastructure and services. It's separate from the royalty paid under your individual lease.

faqs.q: Can you buy an interest that's split among several heirs?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly buy individual heir shares or coordinate a single closing that pays multiple family members according to their confirmed interests.

faqs.q: What documents do you need to make an offer?
faqs.a: A copy of your lease and any recent royalty statements are the most useful starting point. If you don't have them, we can often locate the relevant records ourselves through county sources.

faqs.q: Is there any obligation to sell once you get an offer?
faqs.a: None. We give you a number and an honest explanation of how we got there. What you do with that information is entirely your decision.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Fayette County, PA
items.meta: Fayette County mineral owner? We buy Marcellus, Utica, and legacy gas interests around Uniontown, Connellsville, and the Route 40 corridor. Talk it through, no obligation.

sections.html:
Fayette County land has been worked twice over — first for coal, then for gas — and the paperwork from both eras is usually still sitting in a drawer somewhere in Uniontown or Connellsville.

The owner's grandfather leased ground in Fayette County back when the Connellsville coke ovens were still glowing at night, and by the time gas rigs showed up decades later nobody in the family could find the original severance deed. That's Fayette County in a sentence: layers of history stacked on the same acre, and mineral owners trying to figure out which layer they actually own.

We buy mineral and royalty interests from owners across Fayette County — Uniontown, Fairchance, Farmington, Fayette City, Grindstone, Hopwood, Hiller, and the smaller crossroads in between. If you inherited a fractional interest from a coal-and-gas farm, or you're holding a Marcellus lease that stopped making sense once the deduction line items showed up, we'd like to hear about it.

sections.title: Where Fayette County sits in the Marcellus play
sections.html:
Fayette is on the southern edge of the wet-gas Marcellus fairway that runs through Washington and Greene counties, so activity here has always been a bit more scattered than the core counties next door. Some ground has seen EQT and CNX laterals; other tracts, especially toward the eastern end of the county near the Laurel Highlands, have only ever produced from older, shallower formations like the Oriskany or Elk sands drilled decades before anyone said the word Marcellus.

That mix matters for value. A tract sitting under an active horizontal unit reads very differently than a legacy vertical well that's been stripper-producing since the 1970s. We look at both, because Fayette County owners often hold both kinds of interest in the same family, sometimes on the same parcel.

sections.title: Coal-and-gas severance is the county's signature headache
sections.html:
Because Fayette County was mined so heavily for coal, a huge share of local mineral titles were severed generations ago in deeds that separated coal, oil, gas, and surface rights into different buckets — sometimes with different owners for each. Recorder of Deeds staff in Uniontown see this constantly: an owner comes in wanting to sell 'the minerals' and finds out coal went one direction in 1911 and oil and gas went another in 1940.

If your family's tract has this kind of history, sorting out exactly what interest you hold before you sell protects you from underselling — or from a deal falling apart at closing because the chain of title has a gap nobody caught.

sections.title: Post-production deductions and the impact fee
sections.html:
Fayette County owners with active Marcellus leases have the same complaint the owner hear across southwestern PA: a royalty statement that starts at 1/8 or higher on paper, then gets whittled down by gathering, compression, and dehydration charges before the check ever hits the mailbox. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a 1/8 floor on the gross lease royalty, but it doesn't ban post-production deductions outright, and cases like Kilmer v. Elexco left plenty of room for operators to keep charging them depending on how the lease is worded.

Act 13 impact fees are a separate pot of money — paid by the driller per well, distributed to counties and municipalities for infrastructure and emergency services, not to individual mineral owners. It's worth knowing the difference before you go looking for that money in your royalty statement, because it was never going to show up there.

sections.title: What we actually pay for
sections.html:
We buy producing royalty interests, non-producing minerals under lease, and in some cases unleased mineral acreage, whether it's your full interest or a fractional share inherited alongside cousins. Pricing depends on things that change tract to tract and month to month — well performance, decline curve, lease terms, remaining term on any Act 13-fee wells nearby, and current market activity — so we won't throw out a number before we've looked at your actual documents.

Bring what you have, even if it's incomplete. A lot of Fayette County families are working from a partial abstract, an old lease from a previous generation, or a single royalty check stub. We've pieced together stranger files than that.

faqs.q: You have a coal deed and a separate oil and gas deed for the same land in Fayette County — which one do you buy?
faqs.a: We buy oil, gas, and mineral interests, not coal. If your family's severance split coal from oil and gas generations ago, we'd only be interested in the oil and gas side, and we can help you figure out which document actually controls that interest.

faqs.q: Your well in Fayette County hasn't produced in years. Is your royalty interest worth anything?
faqs.a: Possibly, especially if the lease is still held and the tract sits near active Marcellus development. A shut-in or marginal well doesn't automatically mean the underlying mineral interest has no value — it depends on nearby activity and remaining lease terms, so it's worth a conversation rather than assuming.

faqs.q: What is the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act and does it apply to your lease?
faqs.a: It's a Pennsylvania law setting a 1/8 floor on gross royalty for oil and gas leases signed after it took effect. Older leases may not be covered the same way, and post-production deduction language still varies by lease, which is why we read the actual document rather than assuming a standard result.

faqs.q: Do you need to go through the Fayette County Recorder of Deeds before selling?
faqs.a: We typically pull and review the recorded chain ourselves as part of due diligence, but if you already have deeds, probate records, or a prior title opinion, sharing those upfront speeds things along and helps us give you a more accurate number sooner.

faqs.q: You inherited a fractional interest with several cousins. Can you buy just your share?
faqs.a: Yes. Fractional interests from inherited Fayette County farms are common, and we regularly buy one heir's share without requiring the whole family to sell together.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Lycoming County, PA
items.meta: Own mineral rights in Lycoming County, PA? Learn about dry-gas Marcellus values, post-production deductions, Act 13 fees, and how a fair sale works.

sections.html:
Lycoming County stretches from the West Branch Susquehanna through some of the thickest, most consistently productive dry-gas rock in the entire Marcellus play, with Williamsport sitting at its center as county seat.

Williamsport is best known outside Pennsylvania for the Little League World Series, but inside the state, and especially inside the gas industry, Lycoming County has been known for something else entirely for well over a decade: some of the steadiest, most heavily drilled dry-gas Marcellus acreage anywhere in the Commonwealth. The Lycoming County courthouse record is well worn by comparison to smaller counties nearby, and that record, not the county's reputation, is what should decide what a parcel here is worth.

What follows walks through what actually drives value here, what a royalty statement is probably not telling an owner outright, and what the recorder of deeds in Williamsport can confirm about a specific parcel before any offer is discussed.

sections.title: Why Lycoming Became a Dry-Gas Anchor County
sections.html: Lycoming sits toward the thick, productive core of the dry-gas Marcellus window, and operators including Anadarko in the play's earlier years, and successor operators since, ran extensive horizontal drilling programs through townships across the county. That sustained development means there's real, documented production and royalty history for most areas of the county, rather than speculative interest alone. Unlike wet-gas counties farther southwest, the gas here is almost pure methane, so royalty tracks natural gas pricing directly without a natural gas liquids cushion.

sections.title: The Deduction Problem, in Plain Terms
sections.html: Pennsylvania courts settled the post-production deduction question in Kilmer v. Elexco Land Services, ruling that operators can subtract reasonable gathering, compression, dehydration, and processing costs from your royalty before paying you, unless your specific lease says otherwise. On top of that, the state's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act only requires a floor of one-eighth of production — it doesn't guarantee one-eighth of the wellhead value before those deductions. Put those two things together and a lot of Lycoming County families open a royalty statement expecting one number and see something noticeably smaller. That gap is real, it's legal under current Pennsylvania law, and it's the single biggest source of frustration we hear about from landowners across this county.

sections.title: Act 13 Impact Fees — A Separate Pot of Money
sections.html: Every unconventional well drilled in Lycoming County pays an annual impact fee under Act 13, distributed to the county and to individual municipalities and townships for roads, water and sewer infrastructure, and emergency services. It's worth knowing about because it's a visible, public sign of how much drilling has actually happened in your specific township — but it's important to understand it doesn't go to mineral owners directly. It's a separate mechanism from your royalty, paid by the operator regardless of who owns the minerals.

sections.title: What the Williamsport Courthouse Record Tells Us
sections.html: Before we discuss a number on any Lycoming County parcel, we pull the chain of title at the county recorder's office, check whether the parcel sits inside a filed drilling unit, and if there's an existing lease, we review its specific deduction and royalty language rather than assuming standard terms apply. A lot of older Lycoming County farms passed through multiple generations without formal partition, so it's common to find fractional interests split among cousins who may not even know each other well anymore — we've coordinated plenty of those multi-heir sales and it's routine work for us, not an obstacle.

sections.title: Selling vs. Holding — What Actually Drives That Decision
sections.html: Some Lycoming County families are happy holding a producing interest for the long-term royalty stream, deductions and all. Others look at years of shrinking checks, a well that's declining as most Marcellus wells eventually do, and gas prices that swing lower on a regular cycle, and decide a lump-sum offer priced against current activity makes more sense for their situation. There's no universally right answer — it depends on your finances, your risk tolerance, and how many heirs are involved. We'll walk through the real numbers with you either way, including your well's production trend if it's already producing, rather than pushing you toward a decision that isn't yours to make.

faqs.q: Why does your Lycoming County royalty check look smaller than expected?
faqs.a: Almost always it's post-production deductions — gathering, compression, and processing costs the operator is allowed to subtract under Kilmer v. Elexco unless your lease specifically prohibits it. We can walk through your actual statement line by line.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an impact fee and your royalty?
faqs.a: Act 13 impact fees are paid by the operator to the county and township for infrastructure and services — they're a separate mechanism from your royalty and don't reduce or add to what you're paid directly.

faqs.q: Several of us inherited a share of the same family farm's minerals — can you work with all of us?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly coordinate sales among multiple heirs on a single Lycoming County interest, and each person can decide separately for their own share.

faqs.q: How is dry gas valued differently than wet gas from counties like Washington or Greene?
faqs.a: Dry gas royalty is based on gas volume and price alone, without the additional natural gas liquids revenue wet-gas counties see, so Lycoming County values track natural gas prices directly.

faqs.q: Do you need an attorney to sell a Lycoming County mineral interest?
faqs.a: You're not required to, but for anything involving inherited or fractional ownership, we'd rather you have a title attorney review the offer before signing, and we'll say so upfront rather than discourage it.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Tioga County, PA
items.meta: Own dry-gas Marcellus minerals near Wellsboro or Tioga County's gas belt? We buy directly, explain deductions honestly, and close without games.

sections.html:
Tioga County land has a way of humbling anyone who thinks it's simple. Between the Pine Creek Gorge and the gas belt that runs through the northern townships, no two family tracts here tell quite the same story.

Tioga County sits in the northern tier of Pennsylvania's dry-gas Marcellus window, with Wellsboro as the county seat and a mix of state forest land, working farms, and timber tracts spread across the townships. Shell and Southwestern Energy were among the operators active here during the leasing boom, and while a good chunk of the county's mineral rights sit under land the Commonwealth itself owns through the state forest system, a substantial amount is still held privately by families who've farmed or timbered this ground for generations.

The Marcellus here runs dry, almost pure methane, which means the economics depend heavily on gathering infrastructure and pipeline takeaway capacity rather than natural gas liquids pricing. That infrastructure reality shapes which parts of the county see steady development and which parts have units permitted but sitting quiet, waiting on a pipeline connection that hasn't been built yet.

sections.title: A County Split Between State Forest and Private Land
sections.html:
Tioga State Forest and Tioga-Hammond Lakes take up a meaningful share of the county's acreage, and mineral rights under state forest land are managed separately through the Bureau of Forestry's own leasing program, not by individual owners. If your family's minerals sit under private land near the forest boundary, though, you're dealing with the same ordinary lease, division order, and royalty questions as anyone else in the Marcellus play, just with development sometimes clustered near the edges of the public land where operators have easier surface access.

That patchwork means unit boundaries in Tioga County can look unusual on a map, weaving around forest tracts and following old farm lot lines instead of neat rectangles. It's worth having someone who actually reads Pennsylvania oil and gas plats confirm exactly which unit your parcel falls in before you agree to any number.

sections.title: Post-Production Deductions on Northern Tier Leases
sections.html:
Leases signed in Tioga County during the 2008 to 2010 boom carried the same post-production deduction language common across the northern tier, and after Kilmer v. Elexco upheld that language for leases that allow it, owners here have watched gathering, compression, and transportation costs chip away at royalty checks that already reflect a lower wellhead price than wetter counties see. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act protects the one-eighth floor on the gross value, but it doesn't stop deductions from being applied within that calculation if your lease language permits it.

We've sat across the table from Tioga County families who assumed their royalty would track the headline gas price they saw on the news, only to find their actual check running well below that once the deductions were applied. That gap is one of the most common reasons owners decide it's time to sell rather than keep monitoring a statement they don't fully trust.

sections.title: Act 13 Impact Fees Fund the Townships, Not Your Check
sections.html: Tioga County and its townships have received Act 13 impact fee revenue since 2012, money that goes toward road repair, emergency services, and other local infrastructure strained by well pad traffic and development. That fee comes from the operator to local government and has nothing to do with your personal royalty. We explain this distinction on every county page because it's one of the most common points of confusion we hear from owners across the northern tier.

sections.title: Selling Minerals in Tioga County
sections.html: We start with your deed and any lease or division order paperwork you have, confirm your parcel against current permits and unit filings, and put together a cash offer grounded in what's actually happening on your ground or nearby. If your interest sits near the state forest boundary or in a township with limited pipeline access, we'll tell you honestly how that affects value instead of glossing over it. Closing happens through a title company, with recording handled at the courthouse in Wellsboro.

faqs.q: Do you own minerals under state forest land differently than private land?
faqs.a: Yes. Minerals under Tioga State Forest are managed by the Commonwealth's Bureau of Forestry, not by private owners. If your interest is under private land near the forest, ordinary lease and royalty rules apply to you directly.

faqs.q: Why does gas development seem uneven across Tioga County townships?
faqs.a: Pipeline gathering infrastructure varies significantly by township here. Some areas have strong takeaway capacity and steady development, while others have permitted units still waiting on a pipeline connection.

faqs.q: How do post-production deductions affect a dry-gas county like this one?
faqs.a: Dry gas already sells for less than wet gas per unit, so deductions for gathering, compression, and transportation take a proportionally larger bite out of an already lower wellhead value. Reviewing your lease language is the first step to understanding your specific exposure.

faqs.q: Does the Act 13 impact fee show up on your royalty statement?
faqs.a: No. It's a separate payment from the operator to county and township government and won't appear anywhere on your division order or royalty check.

faqs.q: What if your mineral interest was never surveyed against the current unit?
faqs.a: That's common on older Tioga County tracts. We work with title professionals who can confirm exactly how your legal description maps to the current unit before we finalize any offer.

Canonsburg is bigger and more built up than most towns on this list, but plenty of the older family tracts around its edges still carry mineral rights nobody's fully sorted out.

Canonsburg sits along Chartiers Creek in one of the more developed parts of Washington County, and while the town itself has grown well past its farming roots, the outlying tracts and older family parcels around it are squarely inside the county's Marcellus leasehold. If you own minerals connected to this area, there's a real chance the tract has been part of an active unit for years, quietly generating a royalty check you've never had explained in plain terms.

We've walked through that exact confusion with our own family's holdings, which is why we start every conversation by explaining what the paperwork says, not by pushing a number.

sections.title: Development pressure and mineral value
sections.html:
As towns like Canonsburg grow, surface development can complicate future drilling on specific parcels even while the underlying mineral rights remain fully valid and, in many cases, still tied to production from nearby units. Owners sometimes assume growth near their tract means their minerals are somehow less relevant; usually the opposite is true, since existing units keep producing regardless of what's built on the surface miles away.

This part of the county is in the wet-gas Marcellus fairway, with Range Resources and CNX among the operators holding significant leasehold in the surrounding townships.

Development around the city has been dense and sustained since Range Resources first proved out the wet-gas window here in the mid-2000s, and units in and around Washington have often seen multiple rounds of drilling as operators returned to established pads for infill wells.

Peters Township, where McMurray sits, has changed a lot over the past few decades, subdivisions and shopping centers now cover ground that was farmland when the original mineral severances happened. We buy mineral and royalty interests around McMurray directly. Whether you're the original family that held onto the minerals when the surface sold for development, or you inherited a small interest and aren't sure what it's connected to, we'll help you sort out what you actually have.

sections.title: When Development Outpaces the Mineral Estate

It's common in growing parts of Washington County for oil and gas rights to have been severed from the surface decades before a farm ever became a subdivision. If your family sold surface land around McMurray years ago but kept the minerals, or if you inherited that severed interest, you may own rights under ground you'd never recognize as farmland today.

Operators have continued to develop the Marcellus in this part of Washington County even as the surface use has shifted, running laterals under residential areas from pads sited elsewhere, which is standard practice and doesn't require disturbing homes above.

sections.title: Tracing a Severed Mineral Estate

We research Washington County Recorder of Deeds records to trace exactly when and how minerals were severed from the surface in your family's case, since that history determines what you own today regardless of what's built on top of the land now.

Northern Pennsylvania's dry gas counties tell a different story than the wet gas fairway further southwest, and Wellsboro is right at the center of that story for Tioga County. This is gas that comes out mostly methane, without the ethane and propane that add extra value down south, but the wells here have often been some of the most consistent producers in the whole play.

We break the math down clearly so you can see what your actual net payment reflects, beyond the headline production figures alone.

Connellsville was called the coke capital of the world a century ago, and the mineral deeds written during that boom still govern who owns what underground here today.

There's a particular kind of paperwork tangle that comes with a place like Connellsville, where an entire regional economy was centered on coal and coke before oil and gas ever entered the picture. Deeds from that era severed coal rights aggressively, and oil and gas were sometimes bundled in with the coal reservation, sometimes carved out separately, sometimes never mentioned at all, which under Pennsylvania law can mean they stayed with the surface owner.

sections.title: Why so many owners here still feel shortchanged

Even with heavy production, the post-production deduction issue affects Greene County owners just as much as anywhere else in the state. Pennsylvania's Kilmer v. Elexco ruling lets operators net gathering, compression, and processing costs against your royalty, and in a wet-gas county like this one, that deduction line can be substantial. Add in the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, which sets a legal floor of one-eighth on the gross value before deductions, and you have a system that guarantees you something but leaves a lot of room for the net number to disappoint.

The Marcellus and deeper Utica formations under this part of Westmoreland County have drawn steady operator interest, and pooled units around Millwood may include acreage from several smaller legacy tracts.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Mars, PA
items.meta: Own minerals under farmland near Mars, PA? We buy Butler County Marcellus interests directly, explain your division order, and close on your timeline.

sections.html:
Butler County land north of Pittsburgh has been quietly leased and drilled for a generation, and a lot of the families holding those minerals never planned to be in the gas business.

Mars sits in the northern reach of Butler County, close enough to the Allegheny River corridor that operators have run Marcellus wet-gas pads through the surrounding townships for years without most residents thinking much about it. If your family's name is on a lease from Adams or Cranberry Township, or you inherited a fractional interest from a grandparent's farm that got broken up when the borough grew up around it, you already know how confusing the paperwork gets.

We buy mineral and royalty interests in this part of Butler County directly, no listing, no waiting on a broker to find a buyer. We look at your deed history, your current division order, and whatever royalty statements you have, then make an offer that reflects what the interest is actually doing today, not what someone promised it might do.

sections.title: Butler County's Wet-Gas Window
sections.html:
Butler sits inside the wetter part of the Marcellus fairway, which means production here carries a mix of natural gas, ethane, and propane rather than pure dry gas. That mix matters for pricing because liquids-rich gas gets processed before it's sold, and processing costs are exactly where post-production deductions eat into a royalty check.

Operators active around Mars and neighboring Butler County townships have run multi-well pads with laterals reaching well past a mile, which is why so many small legacy tracts near the borough ended up pooled into units their original owners never signed a lease for directly. If you're holding an interest by inheritance rather than by your own lease, that's a common story here, not an unusual one.

sections.title: What We Look At Before Making an Offer
sections.html:
We start with the Butler County Recorder of Deeds records to confirm the chain of title, then pull your current division order to see what decimal interest you're actually being paid on. A lot of Mars-area interests trace back to farms split among siblings decades ago, so the fractional math can be more complicated than the deed itself suggests.

From there we look at 12 to 24 months of royalty history if you have it. That trailing production tells us far more than a well's original completion numbers, since Marcellus wells decline fast in the first few years and level off afterward.

sections.title: Deductions and the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act
sections.html:
Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a floor at one-eighth of production, but plenty of leases signed before that protection or drafted around it still leave gathering, compression, and dehydration costs coming straight off your check before you see a dollar. If your statement shows deductions eating a large share of gross value, you're not imagining it, and you're not alone in Butler County.

We don't need you to untangle that math yourself. Send us what you have and we'll walk through it with you plainly before any number gets discussed.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests near Mars that are still leased but not yet producing?
faqs.a: Yes. We evaluate leased but non-producing interests based on the operator, the lease terms, and how active drilling has been in that specific township, and we'll tell you honestly if we think waiting makes more sense for you.

faqs.q: You only have a fractional interest inherited from your grandfather's farm. Is that worth anything?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are common around Mars because so much of the original farmland here was subdivided over generations. Even a modest decimal interest tied to an active unit can have real value, so it's worth sending us the details.

faqs.q: How fast can this close?
faqs.a: Once we've confirmed title through the Butler County Recorder of Deeds, most straightforward transfers close within a few weeks. Complicated estates with unresolved probate take longer, and we'll tell you that up front.

items.meta: Lawrenceville, PA sits at the Tioga County border with New York — dry-gas Marcellus on one side, a fracking ban on the other. What that means for you.

sections.html:
Lawrenceville sits at the very edge of Tioga County, close enough to New York that the different rules on each side of the state line are hard to miss.

Drive a few miles north of Lawrenceville and you cross into New York, where high-volume hydraulic fracturing has been banned since 2014. Stay on the Pennsylvania side and you're in dry-gas Marcellus territory that's been actively drilled for well over a decade. That contrast isn't trivia — it's part of why land values and lease activity on the Pennsylvania side of this border have stayed meaningfully different from what New York landowners just across the line have experienced.

sections.html:
Tioga County has seen sustained horizontal Marcellus development for years, with Seneca Resources among the operators active in the area. Lawrenceville-area parcels benefit from that track record — there's usually real nearby production data to reference rather than pure speculation.

Families here sometimes ask whether New York's ban could someday extend into Pennsylvania — it's a fair question, but current Pennsylvania law and regulation govern Lawrenceville minerals, and we base any offer on that reality rather than speculation about future rule changes.

sections.title: What New York's Ban Means (and Doesn't Mean) for You

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Sullivan County, PA
items.meta: Sullivan County minerals leased but never drilled? We buy Marcellus interests here, explain what held-by-production actually means, and pay cash.

sections.html:
Sullivan County is the quiet neighbor in the Marcellus story. It got leased just as hard as Bradford and Susquehanna counties next door, but a lot of that ground has sat undeveloped for years, and that quiet is exactly what confuses owners the most.

Sullivan County is one of the least populated counties in Pennsylvania, tucked into the Endless Mountains with the county seat in Laporte, a borough small enough that most people drive through it without noticing. During the Marcellus leasing rush of the late 2000s, landmen covered this county thoroughly, and thousands of acres got locked into five-year primary terms with the same operators drilling hard in Bradford and Susquehanna counties. But Sullivan County's terrain is steeper, its access roads thinner, and its population base smaller, so a meaningful share of those leases expired or sat quiet while operators concentrated rigs on easier ground nearby.

That history leaves a lot of Sullivan County families in an unusual spot. Some own minerals under an active, producing unit that pays like any other Marcellus interest. Others hold a lease that technically expired years ago and never got formally released, or a fresh lease that's still sitting in its primary term with no well anywhere near it. Knowing which situation you're actually in changes everything about what your interest is worth.

sections.title: Leased Doesn't Always Mean Drilled Here
sections.html:
In a county like Sullivan, the gap between a signed lease and an actual producing well can run years, sometimes indefinitely. If your family signed a Marcellus lease during the boom and no well was ever drilled on your unit before the primary term expired, that lease may no longer be valid at all, which means your minerals could be entirely open to a new lease today. On the other hand, if a well was drilled and completed on your unit before the primary term ran out, most standard leases stay held by production for as long as that well keeps producing, even at modest rates.

We check this first on every Sullivan County inquiry, because it changes the entire conversation. An unleased, open interest in a lightly developed county is worth something different than a producing interest tied to an active unit, and neither number is something you should guess at.

sections.title: The Deduction and Impact Fee Questions Still Apply
sections.html: For the Sullivan County families who do have an active, producing interest, the same statewide rules govern the check. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets the one-eighth floor on gross value, and post-production deductions for gathering and compression can still be applied within that calculation depending on how your specific lease was written, the same Kilmer v. Elexco framework that governs leases across the play. Act 13 impact fees also reach Sullivan County, funding township roads and emergency services, but that money flows from operator to local government, not into your royalty statement.

sections.title: Terrain, Access, and Why Development Has Been Slower Here
sections.html: Sullivan County's steep ridges and state game lands make well pad construction and pipeline routing more expensive than in flatter counties nearby, and that cost difference has kept the pace of drilling here noticeably slower than in Bradford or Susquehanna County even though the rock itself sits in the same dry-gas fairway. Operators have tended to prioritize acreage where infrastructure already exists, which means Sullivan County activity often clusters near the county line where it connects into gathering systems built for the neighboring county's wells.

sections.title: What We Look at Before Making an Offer Here
sections.html: Because status varies so much parcel to parcel in Sullivan County, we spend extra time confirming whether your lease is still in force, whether a well has actually been drilled on your unit, and what the DEP's permit records show for anything nearby. From there we give you a clear, honest number, whether that's for a producing interest, an expired-lease open interest, or something in between. We record every transfer properly with the recorder of deeds in Laporte.

faqs.q: Your family leased minerals in Sullivan County years ago but nothing was ever drilled. Is the lease still active?
faqs.a: Possibly not. Most leases from that era had a five-year primary term, and if no well was drilled and completed before that term expired, the lease likely lapsed. We can help you check the recorder of deeds records to confirm.

faqs.q: If your lease expired, can you still sell your minerals?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Hunker, PA
items.meta: Own mineral rights near Hunker in Westmoreland County? Learn what wet-gas Marcellus interests are worth here and how a fair, no-pressure offer works.

sections.html:
Hunker is a small crossroads community in Sewickley Township, sitting inside one of the wettest, richest parts of the Marcellus fairway in Westmoreland County.

The owner's grandfather signed his first gas lease on a farm not far from Hunker back when a landman still drove out in person and shook your hand at the kitchen table. Sixty years later his grandkids inherited an eighth of the minerals under that same ground, split four ways, and none of us had any idea what it was worth or who to call. That's the situation a lot of Hunker families are sitting in right now — small unincorporated place, big Marcellus wet-gas numbers underneath it, and a deed that hasn't been touched since a great-aunt passed it down.

sections.title: Why Hunker Sits in a Premium Part of the Play
sections.html: Westmoreland County is inside the wet-gas window of the Marcellus, which means the gas coming up here carries natural gas liquids — ethane, propane, butane — alongside the methane. Operators pay more attention to wet-gas acreage than dry-gas acreage because there's a second revenue stream at the processing plant, and that has kept horizontal development active around Sewickley Township for years even when prices dipped elsewhere in the state.

sections.title: What Your Deed Probably Says
sections.html: Most of the older Hunker-area deeds we look at reserved minerals in fractions — a half, a third, sometimes a sixteenth — going back to a farm sale in the early-to-mid 1900s. If your name isn't the only one on the royalty statement, or if the statement lists an old family surname instead of yours, you're probably holding an inherited fractional interest that never went through a formal transfer. That's normal, and it's fixable at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg with the right paperwork.

sections.title: The Post-Production Deduction Problem
sections.html: This is the part that makes people angry, and rightfully so. Pennsylvania operators are allowed to subtract gathering, compression, and processing costs from your royalty before they cut the check, under the standard set by the Kilmer v. Elexco decision — unless your lease specifically forbids it. Combined with the state's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, which only guarantees you a floor of one-eighth, plenty of Hunker landowners open a royalty statement and find a number far smaller than what the wellhead price would suggest. We read that statement line by line before we ever talk numbers with you.
