interest-types.title: Mineral and Royalty Interest Types

items.name: Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own Pennsylvania mineral rights and unsure exactly what that means? We explain ownership, leasing, and royalty basics, then give a straightforward offer.

sections.html:
Owning mineral rights means owning what's underneath the ground, separate and apart from whatever's growing or built on top of it, and that simple fact surprises a lot of Pennsylvania landowners the first time they really think it through.

When our family sold our own minerals, the hardest part wasn't the paperwork - it was understanding what we actually owned in the first place. Mineral rights are the full bundle of ownership in the oil, gas, coal, and other resources beneath a piece of land, and that bundle includes the executive right to negotiate and sign a lease, the right to a bonus payment when you do, delay rentals if the lease calls for them, and a royalty share of anything produced once a well comes online.

That's the broadest, most complete form of subsurface ownership, and it's different from the narrower carved-out interests like an NPRI, ORRI, or working interest, each of which holds only a piece of that full bundle. If you inherited or hold a straightforward mineral interest with no history of it being split into those narrower pieces, this is what you own.

sections.title: The Rights That Come Bundled Together
sections.html:
Full mineral ownership gives you the executive right - the authority to decide whether to lease at all, to whom, and on what terms, which is the piece that carved-out royalty owners like NPRI holders don't have. It also gives you the right to a signing bonus when a lease is executed, delay rental payments if your lease's primary term requires them to keep it active without drilling, and the royalty share of production once a well is drilled and completed.

In Pennsylvania, that bundle also includes practical realities specific to this state - the right to whatever protection the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act provides on your lease's royalty floor, and depending on your specific tract, exposure to Act 13 impact fee considerations that affect local infrastructure funding around your property even though that fee doesn't come out of your royalty directly.

sections.title: How Mineral Ownership Gets Established and Passed Down
sections.html:
Mineral rights are real property in Pennsylvania, conveyed by deed the same as a house or a farm, and they pass through inheritance the same way too - by will, or by intestate succession if there's no will, through the probate process in whatever county the owner resided in. Because Pennsylvania has such a long history of mineral severance going back to the coal era, ownership chains can be genuinely old, sometimes tracing back a century or more through multiple generations of a family, multiple wills, and occasionally a gap or two that takes real courthouse research to close.

This is why title work matters so much before any sale - confirming the actual chain of ownership from the original severance or purchase down to you, through however many transfers happened along the way, is usually the single most involved part of putting together an accurate offer.

sections.title: Producing vs. Non-Producing, and Why That Changes Everything
sections.html:
A producing mineral interest, tied to a well actively generating royalty checks, is valued largely off that actual production and payment history - real numbers, real decline curves, a real track record with a specific operator. A non-producing interest, whether it's never been leased or was leased and the lease expired without a well being drilled, is valued instead off the probability of future development based on nearby activity, permits, and how operators have been expanding leasehold in your county recently.

Both are real, sellable assets, but they require very different approaches to valuation, and anyone offering you a number should be able to explain clearly which category your interest falls into and why that shaped what they're offering.

sections.title: What We Need to Put Together an Offer
sections.html: For a producing interest, we want your division order, lease, and recent royalty statements. For a non-producing interest, we want your deed and whatever ownership documentation establishes your chain of title, plus the county and general location so we can research nearby activity. Either way, we'll walk you through exactly how we arrived at our number, section by section, the same way we'd want it explained if the acreage were ours.

faqs.q: What's the difference between mineral rights and a royalty interest?
faqs.a: Full mineral rights include the executive right to negotiate and sign leases plus bonus, delay rental, and royalty rights. A standalone royalty interest, like an NPRI, is a narrower carve-out with royalty rights only, no executive authority.

faqs.q: How do you find out exactly what you own?
faqs.a: Start with your deed, and any prior deeds in the chain of title at the county recorder of deeds, looking for any reservation, exception, or prior conveyance language that might have carved your interest into something narrower than full mineral ownership.

faqs.q: Do mineral rights expire if they're never leased?
faqs.a: No, mineral ownership itself doesn't expire from lack of leasing in Pennsylvania - it's a permanent property interest that simply sits unleased until you or a future owner decides to lease it, unless a specific deed provision states otherwise.

faqs.q: Can you sell part of your mineral rights and keep the rest?
faqs.a: Yes, partial sales - a percentage interest, specific formations, or a term interest - can often be structured depending on your goals, though most owners choose a full sale for simplicity.

faqs.q: What documents do you need to make an offer on your mineral rights?
faqs.a: For a producing interest, your division order, lease, and recent royalty statements. For a non-producing interest, your deed and ownership documentation, plus the county and location of the acreage.

image.alt: Mineral Rights mineral rights

items.name: Royalty Interests
items.meta: Own a royalty interest tied to a producing Marcellus or Utica well in Pennsylvania? We evaluate your statement history and give a straightforward offer.

sections.html:
A royalty interest is the piece most Pennsylvania mineral owners actually deal with day to day - the check that shows up, the statement full of numbers you have to squint at, the thing your family calls 'the gas money.'

When people say they own mineral rights in Pennsylvania, what they usually mean in practice is that they own a royalty interest tied to a lease on their minerals - the right to a percentage share of production revenue once a well is drilled and producing. That royalty share typically comes bundled with the rest of your mineral estate, unlike a standalone NPRI or ORRI, which means you also had (or have) the right to negotiate the lease itself, receive a signing bonus, and collect delay rentals if the lease requires them.

We look at more royalty statements than almost anyone outside an operator's own accounting department, and the honest truth is most owners never fully understand what they're looking at. Gross value, net value, deductions with abbreviations that mean nothing without a decoder - it's confusing on purpose or by accident, and either way it leaves owners unsure whether their check reflects what it should.

sections.title: Reading Your Own Royalty Statement
sections.html:
Most Pennsylvania royalty statements show a gross production volume and value, then a series of deductions - gathering, compression, dehydration, sometimes fractionation if you're in a wet gas county - before landing on the net amount actually paid to you. Your royalty fraction, usually somewhere around one-eighth in many older leases or higher in more recently negotiated ones, gets applied either to the gross figure or the net figure depending on exactly how your lease's royalty clause was written, and that distinction alone can be worth real money over the life of a well.

If you've never compared your actual royalty fraction against what your statement implies you're receiving after deductions, that's worth doing at least once, particularly if your lease predates the more recent generation of royalty-friendly lease language that many owners negotiated later in the play's development.

sections.title: What Drives Your Royalty Value Beyond the Lease Terms
sections.html:
Two owners with identical royalty fractions on the same lease can still see very different check amounts depending on their net mineral acres within the pooled spacing unit, which well or wells in that unit are actually contributing to their share, and where those wells sit on the production decline curve. A well in its first eighteen months of production behaves completely differently than the same well five years later, and your royalty check reflects wherever in that curve your specific wells currently sit.

Commodity price matters too, obviously, and it's the piece nobody controls. Natural gas prices swing with weather, storage levels, and national supply and demand, and a royalty check can shrink or grow month to month for reasons that have nothing to do with your well's actual production volume.

sections.title: The Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, Plainly
sections.html: Pennsylvania's 1979 Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act requires most oil and gas leases in the state to provide for a royalty of at least one-eighth of gross value received at the wellhead. It doesn't ban post-production deductions outright, but it's been the basis for real disputes over whether certain deduction practices improperly reduce owners below that statutory floor. If your effective royalty, after every deduction is subtracted, looks like it's landed under one-eighth of what the gas actually sold for, that's a conversation worth having with an attorney who handles Pennsylvania royalty disputes specifically, not something to assume is just normal.

sections.title: What a Producing Royalty Interest Is Worth to Sell
sections.html: We build an offer from your actual statement history - typically the last one to two years of checks - combined with the operator's reserve and decline behavior in that specific field, and your lease's royalty and deduction terms. A royalty interest with a strong, consistent payment history from a reliable operator like a major Marcellus player evaluates differently than an interest with sporadic payments or an operator known for slow or inconsistent statements. We'll walk you through exactly how we got to our number, statement by statement, rather than handing you a figure with no explanation.

faqs.q: Why did your royalty fraction change from what you remember signing?
faqs.a: It typically hasn't changed - what shifts is the net amount after deductions, which can make the effective percentage feel different from the stated lease fraction. Compare your gross value line against your net payment to see the actual deduction impact.

faqs.q: Is your royalty applied to gross or net value?
faqs.a: It depends on your specific lease's royalty clause language - some are calculated on gross proceeds at the wellhead, others allow post-production costs to be netted first. Your original lease document will specify which applies.

faqs.q: How many years of statements do you need to make an offer?
faqs.a: Typically the last one to two years gives us enough production and payment history to evaluate the interest accurately, though more history is helpful if you have it.

faqs.q: Does your royalty interest include future wells drilled on the same unit?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if your lease and mineral ownership cover the acreage those future wells would be pooled into, though it depends on your specific lease and deed language.

faqs.q: What if your royalty checks have stopped or gotten inconsistent?
faqs.a: That can happen for several reasons - the well's decline, a change in operator, or an address or ownership record issue on the operator's end. Worth checking your statement history and contacting the operator's royalty department directly to confirm.

image.alt: Royalty Interests mineral rights

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: Own a non-participating royalty interest on Pennsylvania mineral acreage? No lease say, no bonus rights, just royalty. We buy NPRIs and explain the fine print.

sections.html:
An NPRI owner gets a royalty check without ever getting a say in the lease that produced it, which is exactly as frustrating as it sounds when the terms don't work in your favor.

A non-participating royalty interest is a carved-out right to a share of production revenue that comes without the bundle of rights that normally travels with mineral ownership - no right to negotiate or sign the lease, no right to a bonus payment when a new lease is signed, no right to delay rentals. What you keep is purely the royalty share once production starts, which is why it's called non-participating: you don't participate in the leasing decisions that determine how much that royalty is worth.

This gets created a few different ways in Pennsylvania - sometimes a prior owner sold or reserved just the royalty portion of their mineral estate while keeping or selling the executive rights separately, sometimes it's the result of an old family transaction that split the estate this way generations ago. Whatever the origin, if you hold an NPRI, the person or company holding the executive right is the one who negotiated your lease terms, for better or worse.

sections.title: Why NPRI Owners Often Feel Stuck
sections.html:
Because you don't hold the executive right, you had no input on the royalty fraction, the post-production cost language, or which operator got the lease in the first place. If the mineral owner who does hold executive rights negotiated a lease with aggressive deduction language, or leased to an operator with a spotty payment history, you're along for that ride with no ability to have negotiated differently, even though the royalty checks land in your name.

This is one of the more common frustrations we hear from NPRI owners in Pennsylvania's wet gas counties specifically - the executive owner may have prioritized a larger signing bonus over royalty-friendly deduction terms, since they got the bonus and you didn't, and that tradeoff shows up in your royalty statement for the life of the well.

sections.title: How an NPRI's Value Is Different From a Full Mineral Interest
sections.html:
An NPRI is valued purely on its royalty stream - production history, decline curve, the specific royalty fraction you hold, and the lease's cost-sharing terms - without any of the additional value a full mineral or executive interest carries from future bonus potential or leasing control. If the underlying acreage isn't yet leased, an NPRI generally has very limited near-term value, since you have no ability to initiate a lease yourself and can only wait for the executive rights holder to act.

Because of that, NPRI valuation leans heavily on whether there's already a producing lease in place and how that specific lease is written, more so than a full mineral interest evaluation would.

sections.title: The Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act and NPRI Owners
sections.html: Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a floor of one-eighth of gross value received for most oil and gas leases, and that floor applies to the lease itself regardless of how the royalty is subsequently split between different owners, including NPRI holders. If your royalty statement looks like the deductions taken have pushed your effective share below what the underlying lease's royalty fraction should provide, that's worth reviewing, though your specific NPRI conveyance document also matters for exactly how your fraction was carved out and whether it tracks the lease's stated royalty precisely.

sections.title: Selling an NPRI
sections.html: Selling a non-participating royalty interest doesn't require any involvement from whoever holds the executive rights - it's your interest to sell independently. We'll want to see the conveyance document that created your NPRI, since the exact language there determines your royalty fraction and whether it applies to all formations and depths or something more limited, along with production and division order history if the interest is currently producing.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an NPRI and a regular royalty interest from mineral ownership?
faqs.a: Both receive a royalty share of production, but an NPRI is specifically a carved-out interest with no executive rights - no ability to negotiate or sign leases, no bonus payments - while a mineral owner's royalty comes bundled with those additional rights.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate your own lease terms if you only hold an NPRI?
faqs.a: No, the executive rights holder negotiates and signs the lease. As an NPRI owner you receive whatever royalty terms that lease establishes, without input into the negotiation.

faqs.q: Is your NPRI worth much if the underlying acreage isn't leased yet?
faqs.a: Generally limited value in that scenario, since you can't initiate a lease yourself and have to wait for the executive rights holder to act. Value increases substantially once there's an active producing lease in place.

faqs.q: Do you need the executive rights holder's permission to sell your NPRI?
faqs.a: No, an NPRI is your independent property interest and can be sold without their involvement or consent.

faqs.q: How do you find the document that created your NPRI?
faqs.a: It should be recorded at the county recorder of deeds where the mineral acreage sits, typically as a reservation or conveyance in a prior deed. We can help locate it if you don't have a copy.

image.alt: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI) mineral rights

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: Hold an overriding royalty interest tied to a Pennsylvania oil and gas lease? ORRIs end when the lease does. We explain the risk and buy them fairly.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty interest lives and dies with the lease it's attached to, which is the single most important thing to understand before you decide whether to sell or hold one.

An ORRI is a royalty carved out of the working interest under a specific lease rather than out of the mineral estate itself, which makes it fundamentally different from the royalty interests most Pennsylvania mineral owners are used to thinking about. Landmen, geologists, brokers, and sometimes small independent operators end up holding ORRIs as compensation for their role in putting a deal together, and occasionally we see them held by mineral owners who negotiated one as part of a more complex lease arrangement.

The key distinction is that an ORRI doesn't attach to the land itself - it attaches to the lease. When that specific lease terminates, whether the well stops producing in paying quantities or the lease simply expires, the ORRI terminates right along with it. That's very different from a mineral or royalty interest tied to the land, which survives lease after lease indefinitely.

sections.title: Why the Lease-Dependency Matters So Much for Value
sections.html:
Because an ORRI dies when its underlying lease dies, its remaining value is entirely tied to how much longer that specific well or unit is likely to keep producing in paying quantities, plus any realistic chance of additional development under the same lease. A Marcellus well several years into its decline curve, held by an operator with no clear plans for further drilling on that lease, represents an ORRI with a shrinking and finite remaining life - not indefinite like a perpetual mineral interest.

This is the single biggest thing we walk ORRI holders through before making an offer: understanding realistically how many more years of production the underlying lease is likely to support, because that directly caps how much future royalty stream actually exists to value.

sections.title: How ORRIs Typically Come to Exist in Pennsylvania's Shale Plays
sections.html: In the Marcellus and Utica buildout, ORRIs got created in a few common ways - a landman or leasing broker negotiated one as part of assembling acreage for an operator, a small operator carved one out when assigning a lease or working interest to a larger company, or a mineral owner negotiated an override as part of a more complex deal structure rather than a straightforward royalty. If you're holding one and aren't sure exactly how it originated, the assignment document that created it will spell out the specifics - which lease, which formations, what fraction, and any depth or geographic limitations.

sections.title: ORRI vs. NPRI: A Distinction Worth Getting Right
sections.html: People sometimes use these terms interchangeably, but they're structurally different. An NPRI is carved from the mineral estate and survives that specific lease's termination, since it's tied to the land and simply attaches to whatever lease happens to be in place at any given time. An ORRI is carved from the working interest under one specific lease and dies with that lease. If you're not sure which one you hold, the conveyance or assignment document that created your interest will tell you, and it's worth confirming before you make any decisions, since the two are valued very differently.

sections.title: Selling an ORRI Before It Runs Out
sections.html: Because an ORRI's value declines as the underlying lease's remaining productive life shortens, there's a real argument for selling sooner rather than later if you're going to sell at all - waiting years into a well's decline curve means selling what's left of a shrinking asset, versus selling today while more of that remaining production life is still ahead of you. We evaluate the specific well's production history, decline trend, and operator's plans for the lease to put together a number that reflects what's realistically left.

faqs.q: Does your ORRI last forever like a mineral interest does?
faqs.a: No, an ORRI terminates when the underlying lease terminates, whether from the well ceasing production in paying quantities or the lease otherwise expiring. It has no life independent of that specific lease.

faqs.q: What's the real difference between an ORRI and an NPRI?
faqs.a: An NPRI is carved from the mineral estate and tied to the land, surviving lease after lease. An ORRI is carved from the working interest under one specific lease and terminates when that lease does.

faqs.q: How do you know how much longer your ORRI's underlying lease will keep producing?
faqs.a: Review the well's production and decline history, which we can help pull, along with any indication of the operator's plans for further development under that same lease.

faqs.q: Is it better to sell an ORRI early or wait?
faqs.a: Since an ORRI's value is tied to remaining lease life, selling earlier in the well's productive period generally captures more remaining value than waiting until later in the decline curve, though this depends on your specific circumstances.

faqs.q: Can an ORRI cover multiple wells or just one?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on how the assignment or conveyance document that created it was written - some cover a single well, others cover an entire lease or unit with multiple wells. Check your specific document.

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Hold a small working interest in a Pennsylvania Marcellus or legacy well, with real drilling and operating cost exposure? We evaluate WI positions honestly.

sections.html:
A working interest pays more than a royalty, but it also sends you a bill when the well needs work, and that second part is the piece a lot of owners underestimate.

Working interests are less common among the everyday family mineral owners we typically talk to, but they show up more than you'd expect in Pennsylvania, especially tied to older, legacy wells in the northwestern part of the state where small independent operators and even individual investors historically took on working interest positions in shallow oil and gas wells going back generations. Unlike a royalty interest, which is free of operating costs by definition, a working interest owner shares in both the revenue and the actual costs of drilling, completing, and operating the well.

That distinction matters enormously. A royalty check is simple - production revenue times your fraction, minus whatever post-production deductions your lease allows. A working interest is your share of revenue minus your share of the operator's actual costs, which can include everything from routine maintenance to an unexpected workover that generates a bill instead of a check for that month.

sections.title: The Liability Side Nobody Talks About Enough
sections.html:
Holding a working interest means you're exposed to joint operating agreement obligations - if the well needs a costly repair, a new pump, or plugging at the end of its life, your share of that cost is your responsibility regardless of whether you want to pay it. Pennsylvania also has plugging requirements for wells once they stop producing, and a working interest owner can carry exposure to those obligations depending on how the specific well and operating agreement are structured. This is a meaningfully different risk profile than a royalty interest, where the worst outcome is simply a smaller check.

This is especially relevant for legacy working interests in older Upper Devonian and shallow oil wells in counties like Venango, Warren, and McKean, some of which have been producing in small amounts since well before the shale era. Many of these older wells are nearing or past the point where plugging becomes a real, foreseeable cost rather than a distant hypothetical.

sections.title: Why We See Working Interests Concentrated in Legacy Wells
sections.html:
Northwestern Pennsylvania is where American oil drilling started, and a lot of the shallow, low-volume wells drilled in that region over the past century still have small working interest owners attached to them - individuals or families who bought into an operating agreement decades ago, sometimes as an investment, sometimes inherited from a relative who did. These wells produce modestly, a few barrels a day or less in many cases, and the working interest share reflects that modest scale, but the cost exposure doesn't scale down the same way small revenue does.

If you've inherited a working interest like this and have been getting occasional joint interest billing statements you don't fully understand, that's a common situation, and it's worth having someone look at the actual operating agreement to understand what obligations come with it.

sections.title: Valuing a Working Interest Correctly
sections.html:
Because a working interest carries cost exposure, it has to be valued net of that exposure, not only off gross revenue the way a royalty would be. We look at the well's production and cost history together, the operating agreement's specific terms, and realistically how much longer the well is likely to produce before plugging becomes the dominant cost consideration. A working interest in a well nearing the end of its economic life can actually carry negative expected value once plugging liability is weighed in, which is important to understand honestly rather than assuming any working interest is automatically an asset worth something.

We'll tell you plainly if that's the situation with a specific interest, because walking someone into a sale that doesn't actually solve their liability exposure isn't something we're willing to do.

sections.title: Selling a Working Interest and What It Resolves
sections.html: Selling transfers both the revenue share and the cost and liability exposure to the buyer, which for a lot of working interest owners is the real appeal - not only the cash from the sale, but no longer being on the hook for joint interest billings, workover costs, or eventual plugging obligations tied to a well you may have never even seen in person.

faqs.q: What's the real difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A royalty interest receives revenue free of operating costs. A working interest receives revenue but also shares in the actual costs of drilling, operating, and eventually plugging the well, which can mean bills instead of checks in some periods.

faqs.q: Am you liable for plugging costs if you hold a small working interest?
faqs.a: Potentially, depending on how your specific operating agreement is structured and the well's status. This is a real risk worth understanding clearly, particularly for older legacy wells nearing the end of their productive life.

faqs.q: Why do you keep getting billing statements instead of royalty checks?
faqs.a: That's typical of a working interest position - you're periodically billed your proportional share of operating costs under the joint operating agreement, separate from and sometimes exceeding your share of revenue in a given period.

faqs.q: Is a working interest in an old legacy well worth anything?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific well's production, remaining life, and cost structure. Some older, low-volume interests carry limited or even negative expected value once plugging liability is factored in, and we'll tell you honestly if that's the case.

faqs.q: Does selling a working interest end your liability for future costs on that well?
faqs.a: Yes, a sale transfers both the revenue rights and the associated cost and liability exposure to the buyer, which resolves your ongoing obligation under the operating agreement.

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: Confused whether you own the surface, the minerals, or both on your Pennsylvania land? We explain the split estate and buy mineral rights either way.

sections.html:
Owning the farm doesn't automatically mean owning what's underneath it, and in Pennsylvania that surprises more landowners than you'd think.

Pennsylvania has one of the oldest histories of mineral rights severance in the country, going back to the coal era in the 1800s when landowners routinely sold off the coal, oil, and gas beneath their farms while keeping the surface to live on and work. That practice created what's called a split estate - the surface and the minerals owned separately, sometimes by completely unrelated parties, sometimes because a family sold the minerals generations ago and simply forgot, sometimes because a family kept the minerals and sold the surface instead.

If you own a farm in Marcellus or Utica country and you're not sure whether you actually own what's underneath it, you're not alone. We talk to landowners regularly who assumed they owned their minerals simply because they owned the land, only to find a deed from decades or even a century ago that severed the mineral estate entirely.

sections.title: How to Actually Check What You Own
sections.html:
The only reliable way to know is to check your deed, and often the deeds before it going back through the chain of title, at the county recorder of deeds. Look for a reservation or exception clause - language like 'excepting and reserving all coal, oil, gas, and other minerals' - in your deed or any prior deed in the chain. If that language exists anywhere in the chain, the minerals were severed at that point and didn't pass with the surface from then forward, regardless of how many times the surface itself has changed hands since.

This is common enough in Pennsylvania, particularly in the older coal counties and parts of the state where land changed hands multiple times through the 1800s and early 1900s, that we always recommend checking before assuming either way. A title search, which we can help facilitate, will trace this definitively.

sections.title: If You Own the Surface But Not the Minerals
sections.html:
This is its own frustrating situation - an operator can generally access the minerals beneath your surface under the reasonable use doctrine even without your consent, since Pennsylvania law generally treats the mineral estate as dominant over the surface estate for purposes of extracting it, though operators still typically need to compensate you for actual surface damage and disruption. If you're in this position, you don't own mineral rights to sell, but you may have separate rights and considerations around surface use agreements when an operator wants to build access roads, well pads, or pipelines on your land.

That's a different conversation from what we typically handle - we buy mineral and royalty interests, not surface use negotiations - but it's worth understanding the distinction clearly so you're not confused about what you can and can't control.

sections.title: If You Own the Minerals But Not the Surface
sections.html: This happens too, particularly with families whose ancestors sold off farmland decades ago but specifically reserved the mineral rights before doing so. If that's your situation, you own a real, valuable asset even though you have no connection to the surface anymore and may not even know exactly where the land is beyond a legal description in an old deed. These interests are fully sellable the same as any other mineral interest, and the fact that you don't own the surface doesn't diminish the mineral estate's value at all.

sections.title: If You Own Both
sections.html: Owning both surface and minerals gives you the most straightforward position - full control over leasing decisions and the benefit of any surface use compensation negotiations if a well gets sited on your land. It also means, if you decide to sell your minerals, you can choose to sell only the mineral estate while keeping the surface, which is what most owners in this position actually do, since the land itself often carries family or practical value the minerals underneath it don't share.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your mineral rights were severed from your surface?
faqs.a: Check your deed and prior deeds in the chain of title at the county recorder of deeds for reservation or exception language covering coal, oil, gas, or minerals. A title search can trace this definitively if your own copies are incomplete.

faqs.q: Can an operator drill under your land if you only own the surface?
faqs.a: Generally yes, Pennsylvania law typically treats the mineral estate as dominant, allowing reasonable use of the surface to access minerals, though the operator usually owes compensation for actual surface damage.

faqs.q: If you own minerals but sold the surface, is your interest still worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes, mineral interests are valued and sold independently of surface ownership - not owning the land above doesn't reduce what the mineral estate underneath is worth.

faqs.q: Can you sell just your minerals and keep your surface land?
faqs.a: Yes, this is common and straightforward - mineral and surface estates can be conveyed separately, so selling your mineral rights doesn't require selling or affecting your surface ownership.

faqs.q: Why would your ancestors have sold the minerals but kept the farm?
faqs.a: This was common historically, particularly during Pennsylvania's coal era, when landowners needed cash and buyers wanted mineral rights without the burden of managing surface farmland, so the two got split by agreement.

basins.title: Pennsylvania Producing Formations

items.name: Marcellus Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own Marcellus Shale minerals or royalties in Washington, Greene, Susquehanna, or Bradford County? Get a fair, no-pressure cash offer from a family that sold too.

sections.html:
The Marcellus is the reason most Pennsylvania mineral owners have a royalty check to complain about at all, and it's also the reason so many of those checks are smaller than they should be.

The owner's grandfather used to say the Marcellus was 'the shale that finally paid,' and for a lot of families in southwestern and northeastern Pennsylvania, that's true. Wells that started producing in the late 2000s and into the 2010s turned quiet farm ground into gas country almost overnight. But owning a piece of the Marcellus isn't the same everywhere in the state, and it isn't the windfall the early news stories made it sound like.

In Washington, Greene, and Fayette counties you're sitting on wet gas and natural gas liquids, which means more processing, more midstream fees, and more line items subtracted before a royalty ever reaches your mailbox. Up in Susquehanna, Bradford, Tioga, and Lycoming counties it's mostly dry gas, fewer deductions, but a royalty stream that lives and dies with the Henry Hub price. We buy and evaluate Marcellus mineral and royalty interests across both regions, and we've learned that owners in each one are frustrated for different reasons.

sections.title: Wet Gas Counties vs. Dry Gas Counties
sections.html:
Southwestern Pennsylvania's Marcellus is liquids-rich, which sounds like a good thing until you see your division order statement. Ethane, propane, and butane have to be separated out at a processing plant before the residue gas gets to market, and operators like Range Resources, EQT, and CNX pass a share of those gathering, compression, dehydration, and fractionation costs back to royalty owners as post-production deductions. Depending on your lease language, those deductions can eat a real chunk of the top-line value before you ever see a number.

Head northeast into Susquehanna, Bradford, or Wyoming County and the picture changes. That's dry gas territory, dominated by Coterra (the old Cabot Oil & Gas leases) and a handful of others, and while post-production costs still show up, there's no fractionation plant taking a cut. What both regions share is a decline curve: Marcellus horizontal wells drop off fast in the first two to three years, then flatten into a long, low tail. If your royalty check today looks a lot smaller than it did five years ago, that's usually the well doing exactly what shale wells do, not evidence something was done wrong.

sections.title: Spacing Units and Why Your Acreage Might Be Pooled with Neighbors
sections.html:
Marcellus horizontal laterals commonly run 5,000 to 10,000 feet and cross multiple original farm tracts, which means your mineral interest is likely pooled into a spacing unit with several neighboring parcels rather than tied to one single well pad. That's normal, and it's part of why two owners on the same road can have wildly different royalty amounts even when they're in the same unit - the split depends on your net mineral acres relative to the whole unit, not only where your fence line sits.

If you've never pulled your division order or gone through the well's production history on the DEP's oil and gas reporting site, that's worth doing before you make any decision about your interest. It tells you which wells are actually draining your unit, roughly where they sit in the decline curve, and whether there's undrilled acreage nearby that could still see activity.

sections.title: Act 13, Impact Fees, and What They Don't Cover
sections.html:
Pennsylvania never passed a severance tax on Marcellus gas the way West Virginia or Texas taxes production. Instead, the 2012 Act 13 impact fee charges drillers a flat per-well fee that scales down over the life of the well and gets distributed to counties and municipalities for roads, water systems, and emergency services. That fee doesn't touch your royalty check one way or the other - it's a separate pot of money that goes to local government, not to mineral owners. We mention it because a lot of families assume Act 13 money is somehow tied to their royalty, and it isn't.

What does touch your check is the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, the 1979 state law that requires most PA oil and gas leases to pay a royalty of at least one-eighth of gross value received at the wellhead. Some operators have tried to net post-production deductions against that floor in ways owners believe violate the law's intent, and it's been the subject of real litigation in this state. If your royalty statement looks like it's dipped under that one-eighth line after deductions, that's worth reviewing with an attorney who handles PA oil and gas leases specifically.

sections.title: What Buyers Actually Look At
sections.html:
When we evaluate a Marcellus interest, we're looking at which operator holds the lease, how far along the well or wells are on the decline curve, whether there's remaining undeveloped acreage in your unit that could get drilled or refractured, and how clean the title is going back through the chain of ownership. A producing interest with a strong operator and several years of consistent royalty history evaluates very differently than a non-producing interest that's only ever been leased and never drilled.

None of that means every offer you get is fair. We've seen buyers lowball owners who don't have their own production data, and we've seen owners turn down reasonable offers because a cold-call letter quoted a number with no basis behind it. We'll walk you through what we're looking at and why, the same way we'd want it explained to us.

faqs.q: Why is your Marcellus royalty check smaller than your neighbor's?
faqs.a: It usually comes down to your net mineral acres inside the pooled spacing unit, your specific lease's royalty fraction and post-production cost language, and which wells in the unit are actually producing. Two neighbors can own the same acreage size and still see very different checks.

faqs.q: Does Act 13 impact fee money go to mineral owners?
faqs.a: No. Act 13 impact fees are paid by the operator on a per-well basis and distributed to county and municipal governments and state agencies for infrastructure and services. It's entirely separate from royalty payments to mineral owners.

faqs.q: Is southwestern PA Marcellus gas worth more than northeastern PA gas?
faqs.a: It depends on the year and the market. Wet gas in the southwest carries natural gas liquids value but also more processing deductions; dry gas in the northeast has fewer deductions but tracks the Henry Hub price directly. Neither region is reliably 'worth more' - it varies with commodity pricing and your specific lease terms.

faqs.q: Can you sell just your Marcellus rights and keep other formations?
faqs.a: In some cases yes, if your deed and lease language allow splitting by formation or depth, though it's less common than a full mineral or royalty sale. We can look at your documents and tell you what's actually possible for your specific interest.

faqs.q: Your well hasn't been drilled yet - can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes, non-producing leased acreage in an active Marcellus play still has value tied to the likelihood of future development, though it typically evaluates lower than a producing interest with royalty history.

items.name: Utica Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own deep Utica or Point Pleasant mineral rights in southwestern Pennsylvania? We evaluate stacked-lateral interests fairly and explain the deductions honestly.

sections.html:
The Utica sits thousands of feet below the Marcellus in most of Pennsylvania, and a lot of owners don't even know they have rights in it until a landman shows up asking about a second lease.

We get calls fairly often from families who leased their Marcellus rights years ago and assumed that was the whole story, only to find out an operator wants a separate lease or a formation amendment for the deeper Utica and Point Pleasant zone underneath it. In Pennsylvania, the Utica play is concentrated in the same southwestern counties as the wet-gas Marcellus - Greene, Washington, Beaver, and parts of Fayette and Westmoreland - and it's a dry, high-pressure gas zone that's been developed more slowly and more selectively than the shale above it.

That slower pace is the biggest thing to understand about a Utica interest here. Unlike West Virginia and eastern Ohio, where the Utica has seen heavy drilling for over a decade, Pennsylvania's Utica activity has stayed limited to a smaller set of deep, expensive wells drilled mostly by operators willing to take on the technical risk of a formation that sits 10,000 to 12,000 feet down. That changes how a Utica interest here should be evaluated compared to one across the state line.

sections.title: A Different Rock, A Different Well Design
sections.html:
Point Pleasant, the interval most operators actually target within the Utica, is a tighter, more overpressured formation than the Marcellus, and completing a well in it costs meaningfully more - deeper vertical section, higher pressure equipment, longer laterals in some cases. Because of that cost, operators have been choosier about where they drill Utica wells in Pennsylvania, generally sticking to acreage where they already have Marcellus infrastructure in place so they can stack the wells on existing pads and share gathering lines.

That stacking matters for owners. If your acreage already has a producing Marcellus well pad on it, the marginal cost for an operator to add a Utica well nearby is lower, which can make your deep rights more attractive to a buyer than an identical parcel with no existing pad. It's one of the first things we check when someone asks us to look at Utica acreage.

sections.title: Undeveloped Utica Rights Are a Different Animal Than Producing Marcellus
sections.html:
A lot of what we see in this play isn't producing at all - it's leased-but-undrilled Utica rights sitting under acreage where the Marcellus has already been developed. That's a legitimate asset, but it prices very differently than a royalty interest with three or four years of check history behind it. We're valuing the likelihood of future development based on operator activity in the area, permit filings, and how close nearby stacked-lateral pads are, not a guaranteed outcome.

Some owners get a lease bonus for the deep rights and figure that's the end of it, not realizing the lease itself, and the right to future royalty if the well is ever drilled, is something that can be sold separately from a producing Marcellus royalty on the same land. If you're holding both, you don't have to sell them together.

sections.title: Post-Production Costs Look Different Down Here Too
sections.html:
Because most Pennsylvania Utica gas is dry and travels through the same wet-gas-region gathering systems as the Marcellus above it, the post-production deduction story is similar to what southwestern PA Marcellus owners already deal with - gathering, compression, and dehydration fees taken before the royalty math happens. The Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act still applies to Utica leases signed on Pennsylvania land the same way it applies to Marcellus leases, and the same one-eighth floor is supposed to hold regardless of formation.

Where it gets confusing is when a single lease or unit covers both formations and the royalty statement lumps deductions together without separating which well the costs came from. If you can't tell from your statement whether a deduction is tied to your Marcellus production or your Utica production, that's worth asking the operator's royalty department to itemize directly, in writing.

sections.title: What We Look At Before Making an Offer
sections.html:
For a producing Utica interest, we look at the well's decline history, the operator, whether it's stacked with existing Marcellus infrastructure, and how the lease's cost-sharing language is written. For non-producing Utica rights, we look at nearby permit activity, whether the surrounding acreage already has pads in place, and how active the specific operator has been in that formation over the last few years, since Utica development in Pennsylvania has stayed more concentrated than the broader Marcellus buildout.

We'll tell you plainly if we think an interest is too early-stage to be worth much right now versus one that's sitting in an area where activity looks likely. That's not the answer every buyer gives, but it's the one we'd want if the acreage were ours.

faqs.q: Do you automatically own Utica rights if you own Marcellus mineral rights?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if your original mineral deed conveyed all formations and depths rather than a specific named zone. Some older leases or deeds do carve out formations by name or depth, so it's worth checking your actual deed language rather than assuming.

faqs.q: Why hasn't your Utica acreage been drilled yet if your Marcellus well is producing?
faqs.a: Utica wells in Pennsylvania cost significantly more to drill and complete than Marcellus wells, so operators have been selective, often waiting to stack Utica laterals with existing Marcellus pads rather than drilling standalone deep wells.

faqs.q: Is Pennsylvania's Utica play as active as Ohio's or West Virginia's?
faqs.a: No, it's been developed more slowly and in a smaller geographic footprint, concentrated mainly in Greene, Washington, and Beaver counties, which affects how quickly undeveloped Utica rights are likely to see activity.

faqs.q: Can you sell your Utica rights but keep your producing Marcellus royalty?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, since they're often severable formation rights even when they sit under the same surface acreage. We can review your deed and lease to tell you what's actually possible.

faqs.q: What if your Utica acreage has never been leased at all?
faqs.a: Unleased deep rights still have value, generally tied to nearby operator activity and whether your tract sits in an area likely to be pooled into a future unit, though it evaluates differently than leased or producing acreage.
