items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: A plain-English walk through your Pennsylvania royalty statement, including why post-production deductions eat into the check and how to check the math.

sections.html:
The owner's grandfather used to hold his statement up to the kitchen light like it might explain itself. It never did.

The first time a royalty statement showed up in our mailbox, the owner's dad set it on the table and just looked at it for a while. Decimal interest, gross value, a column of deductions with names like gathering, compression, and dehydration, then a number at the bottom that never matched what we thought we'd get. We weren't confused because we were bad at math. We were confused because the form is built for an operator's accounting system, not for a family trying to understand what happened to their gas.

This guide breaks the statement down section by section the way we eventually learned to read it ourselves, after a few phone calls to the operator and a conversation with a landman who was more patient than most. If you own minerals or royalty in the Marcellus or Utica in Pennsylvania, this is the document that tells you the truth about what your interest is actually producing, and where the money goes before it gets to you.

sections.title: The columns that actually matter
sections.html:
Most PA statements run the same basic columns: production month, product (gas, sometimes NGLs or condensate), gross volume, price, gross value, your decimal interest, deductions, and net paid. The decimal interest is your slice of the well, usually a long string like 0.00041273. It comes from your net mineral acres divided by the spacing unit acreage, multiplied by your royalty fraction. If that number ever changes without an explanation, it's worth a call, because it usually means the unit was repooled or another owner's interest was reallocated.

Gross value is the volume times the price before anything is subtracted. Net paid is what actually lands in your account. The gap between those two numbers is where post-production deductions live, and in Pennsylvania that gap has been a source of real frustration for royalty owners for years.

sections.title: Post-production deductions, explained honestly
sections.html:
Here's the part that made the owner's dad set the statement down. Gas doesn't arrive at your royalty check the way it comes out of the ground. It has to be gathered, compressed, dehydrated, and sometimes processed before it can be sold at the point operators use to value it. In Pennsylvania, many older leases use "at the well" royalty language, and courts here, going back to the Kilmer decision, have generally allowed operators to deduct a proportionate share of those post-production costs from the royalty owner's check, even when the lease doesn't spell it out in detail.

That means two neighbors with the same well and different lease language can see different net numbers on paper for the same gross production. It isn't a mistake on the statement, but it is exactly the kind of thing that makes owners feel like they're not getting the full picture. If your deductions line item is a large percentage of gross value, that's worth understanding before you decide whether to lease, sell, or just live with it, because it directly affects what your interest is worth to a buyer evaluating future cash flow.

sections.title: What to do if the numbers don't add up
sections.html:
Start by comparing your decimal interest across a few months. It should stay flat unless there's a formal reallocation, and the operator should be able to explain any change in writing. Next, check whether the deduction categories are consistent month to month; a sudden jump in "gathering" costs with no new infrastructure nearby is a fair question to ask.

If you inherited the interest, statements sometimes still carry a prior owner's decimal or an old address, which slows everything down and can even suspend payment until title is cleared. Keep every statement you receive, even the confusing ones, because a buyer evaluating an offer on your minerals will want a run of recent statements to judge how the well is declining and how heavy the deductions are running.

faqs.q: Why did your royalty check drop even though gas prices went up?
faqs.a: Price is only one input. If volumes declined that month, or post-production deduction costs rose, the net paid can fall even in a month when the posted gas price was higher. Compare gross value and deductions side by side rather than just looking at the check amount.

faqs.q: Can an operator legally deduct post-production costs in Pennsylvania?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes, when the lease uses "at the well" or similarly silent royalty language, based on how Pennsylvania courts have interpreted these leases. Some newer leases negotiate a "no deductions" clause, which is why lease language varies so much between neighbors.

faqs.q: What's a division order and does it change your royalty?
faqs.a: A division order confirms your decimal interest for payment purposes; it shouldn't change the royalty rate set in your lease or deed. Read it against your own records before signing, and ask questions about anything that doesn't match what you expect.

faqs.q: Do you need a CPA to make sense of these statements?
faqs.a: For the deductions and volumes, no, this guide covers the mechanics. For how the income affects your taxes, talk to your CPA or tax advisor, since royalty income is treated differently than a lump-sum mineral sale.

faqs.q: Does a heavy deduction line mean your minerals are worth less?
faqs.a: It can affect how a buyer values future royalty income, since deductions reduce net cash flow, but the underlying reserves and well performance still matter most. A buyer weighing an offer on your interest should be looking at both.

image.alt: Reading Your Royalty Statements mineral rights

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: What a Pennsylvania division order actually is, why it shows up after you inherit or sell an interest, and what to check before you sign one.

sections.html:
The envelope looked official enough that the owner's aunt almost signed it at the kitchen counter before reading a word.

A division order is one of those documents that arrives with no context, usually right after a new well is completed, an interest changes hands through inheritance, or a title company finishes clearing up an estate. It's easy to assume it's just paperwork the operator needs, sign and move on. Most of the time that's close to true, but not always, and the exceptions are worth knowing before you put your name on anything tied to a decimal interest and a royalty rate.

We've had division orders come through our own family more than once, once after the owner's grandfather passed and the interest split between his children, and again years later when a producer redrew a spacing unit. Each time it took a phone call to confirm the numbers actually matched what we expected. This guide walks through what the document is, what it isn't, and what to check before you sign.

sections.title: What a division order actually does
sections.html:
A division order is the operator's way of confirming, on paper, exactly what decimal share of a well's production belongs to you before they start cutting checks. It typically lists the well name, the county and formation, your decimal interest, and sometimes the royalty rate carried over from your lease or deed. Signing it tells the operator you agree the numbers are correct so they can begin or continue payment without holding funds in suspense.

It is not a new contract that overrides your lease or deed, and it shouldn't be used to quietly change your royalty rate or add new deduction language. If a division order shows a royalty percentage that doesn't match your lease, that's a red flag worth raising before you sign, not after the first check arrives short.

sections.title: Why they show up after inheritance or a title change
sections.html:
Operators need a clean chain of title to know who to pay, and a division order is often the trigger point for updating their records. If you inherited a fractional interest, expect the operator to ask for a certified death certificate, sometimes a probate or estate closing document, and proof of how the interest was distributed among heirs before they'll issue a new division order in your name.

Until that paperwork clears, payment on your share is usually held in suspense rather than paid to the wrong person, which is frustrating but generally protects you from having to claw money back from someone else's account. It's also exactly the kind of delay that pushes some heirs, especially ones scattered across multiple states, toward selling the interest outright rather than managing the ongoing title and paperwork.

sections.title: What to check before you sign
sections.html:
Compare the decimal interest against your own calculation if you have your net mineral acres and the spacing unit size. Confirm the well name and county match what you actually own, since clerical mix-ups between similarly named wells do happen. Check the royalty rate against your original lease or deed language, and if there's a deduction clause referenced, read it against what your royalty statements have actually been showing.

If anything looks off, call the operator's division order department before signing, not after. Most division orders don't have a strict deadline that forfeits your interest if you take a few extra days to verify the numbers, so there's rarely a reason to rush.

sections.title: When a division order surfaces during a sale
sections.html:
If you're selling a producing interest, expect the buyer's closing team to ask for copies of any division orders you've signed, along with recent statements, because those documents help confirm exactly what decimal share is changing hands. After closing, the buyer typically sends the operator a new division order request along with the recorded deed, so future payments route correctly.

This step is one reason a producing sale sometimes takes a few extra weeks compared to unleased acreage; operators have their own internal timelines for processing new division orders once they receive a recorded deed, and that's outside anyone's direct control.

faqs.q: Do you have to sign a division order to get paid?
faqs.a: Most operators require a signed division order before releasing regular payment, though some will pay for a limited period without one. If you're unsure, ask the operator directly what their policy is rather than assuming.

faqs.q: Does a division order change your royalty rate?
faqs.a: It shouldn't. It's meant to confirm your existing decimal interest and royalty rate from your lease or deed, not renegotiate them. If the number differs from your lease, question it before signing.

faqs.q: What happens if you never sign it?
faqs.a: Payment on your interest is typically held in suspense until the paperwork is resolved, which can mean months of delayed royalty checks. It doesn't usually cause you to lose the underlying mineral interest itself.

faqs.q: Why did your decimal interest change on a new division order?
faqs.a: This usually happens after a spacing unit is repooled, a new well is added to the unit, or another owner's title issue was resolved. The operator should be able to explain the change in writing if you ask.

faqs.q: Will selling your interest affect a division order already in place?
faqs.a: Yes, once a sale closes and the deed records, the buyer typically requests a new division order in their name so payments route correctly going forward, replacing your prior one.

image.alt: Division Orders Explained mineral rights

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: The paperwork a Pennsylvania mineral owner actually needs before selling, from the original deed to recent royalty statements, and where to find each one.

sections.html:
We dug through a filing cabinet in the owner's mother's basement for three weekends before we found the original deed.

Nobody hands you a folder labeled mineral rights paperwork when they leave you an interest in the ground. Most families end up with a shoebox, a filing cabinet, or a lawyer's storage unit somewhere, and figuring out what's actually needed to move a sale forward can feel like its own project on top of everything else. We've been through this ourselves, tracking down a deed that had been recorded under a maiden name from three generations back.

This checklist covers what a buyer or title company will actually ask for in Pennsylvania, in roughly the order it tends to come up, so you're not scrambling for the same document twice.

sections.title: The core ownership documents
sections.html:
Start with anything establishing how you came to own the interest: the original mineral deed or reservation, or if you inherited it, the will, probate record, or estate closing documents, plus a death certificate if the prior owner has passed. If the interest passed through more than one generation without formal probate, that gets more complicated and often needs an heirship affidavit or a quiet title action to clear, which is common enough in rural Pennsylvania counties that most local title examiners have seen it before.

If you have a survey or plat showing your mineral acreage within a specific tract, bring it, though many older deeds in Pennsylvania describe boundaries by metes and bounds referencing long-gone landmarks rather than a modern survey, and that's normal, not a defect.

sections.title: Lease and production paperwork
sections.html:
If your minerals are currently leased, bring a copy of the lease itself, including any addenda or amendments, since royalty rate and deduction language live there and a buyer will want to see it. If a well is producing on your interest, gather your last twelve to twenty-four months of royalty statements, since decline trends and average monthly volume are central to how an offer gets built.

Include any division orders you've signed, correspondence with the operator about suspended payments or title issues, and, if you have it, a copy of the well's API number or unit designation. None of this needs to be perfectly organized; a buyer's team is used to working through a messy pile.

sections.title: Tax and county records worth pulling
sections.html:
A recent county tax assessment on the mineral interest, where the county tracks it separately from surface land, helps confirm the parcel is correctly identified. If you've received a 1099 for royalty income in recent years, that's useful backup for production history even without the original statements.

If title has never formally passed to you and you're still listed under a parent's or grandparent's name at the courthouse, say so upfront rather than after an offer is made; it's common in Pennsylvania's older mineral records and doesn't kill a deal, but it does affect the timeline.

sections.title: A few things worth pulling even if nobody asked
sections.html:
Old family correspondence about the property, even a letter mentioning a lease bonus check from decades ago, can help a title examiner piece together a chain of ownership that the recorded documents alone don't fully explain. If a relative kept notes on which children inherited which fraction, bring those too, even informal ones.

If you've ever received a permit notice, a pooling notice, or correspondence from an operator about a new well nearby, keep it. These documents sometimes contain the well name or unit information that speeds up matching your interest to current production, especially if your own records only reference the original deed acreage.

faqs.q: What if you can't find the original deed?
faqs.a: A title examiner or the county recorder of deeds can usually pull a copy from the courthouse records using your name, the prior owner's name, or the property description. It's slower but rarely a dead end in Pennsylvania counties.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to gather these documents?
faqs.a: Not necessarily for gathering them, but if title passed through multiple generations without formal probate, an attorney familiar with Pennsylvania heirship can save real time clearing it before closing.

faqs.q: What if your minerals aren't currently leased or producing?
faqs.a: You can still sell an unleased interest; you'll just have less production paperwork to provide, and the offer will be based more on the deed, acreage, and local activity than on royalty history.

faqs.q: How long does it usually take to gather everything?
faqs.a: Straightforward title with a clear deed can come together in days. Estates that never went through probate, or interests split across several heirs, often take several weeks to sort out fully.

faqs.q: Should you get copies made before mailing originals anywhere?
faqs.a: Yes, always keep copies of original deeds, wills, or probate records for your own file before sending anything to a buyer or title company, even if they request originals for review.

faqs.q: What if your documents are scattered across several relatives?
faqs.a: That's common with older mineral interests. Start a shared folder or even a group text where everyone drops photos of what they have; a title examiner can usually piece together a full chain from partial records held by different family members.

image.alt: Documents You Need to Sell mineral rights

items.name: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
items.meta: The warning signs of a lowball mineral rights offer in Pennsylvania, from unsolicited flat-rate letters to pressure tactics, and what a fair offer looks like.

sections.html:
The owner's father kept a stack of unsolicited offer letters in a drawer for years, mostly because throwing them away felt like giving up leverage.

If you own minerals in Pennsylvania, you've probably gotten a letter or a postcard offering to buy your interest for a flat number, sometimes before you've even confirmed what you own with them. Some of these are legitimate businesses making a fair first offer. Others are testing whether an owner will sign something without asking questions. Telling the two apart isn't always obvious, but there are patterns worth knowing.

We've had our own family members receive these letters, and the ones that felt off shared a few things in common. Here's what to watch for.

sections.title: Flat, unsolicited numbers with no paperwork review
sections.html:
A genuine offer usually comes after someone has looked at your deed and, if applicable, your royalty statements. A number that arrives before anyone has reviewed anything specific to your ownership is often built off a flat county-wide rate applied to whatever acreage figure the sender pulled from public records, which can be wrong, outdated, or simply not reflective of your actual decimal interest or lease terms.

That doesn't automatically make it a scam, but it's a starting point, not a final answer, and it's worth treating it that way rather than signing back a form that locks in the first number offered.

sections.title: Pressure to sign quickly, and vague explanations
sections.html:
Watch for language pushing you to respond within a very short window, or offers that expire the moment you ask a follow-up question. A legitimate buyer should be able to explain, in plain terms, how they arrived at their number, what recent activity in your area supports it, and should be comfortable with you taking time to review your own paperwork or run the offer past someone else.

Also watch for documents that bundle in language beyond a simple sale, granting broad additional rights, waiving future claims, or including surface access terms that go further than what you intended to sell. Read anything you're asked to sign fully, and if it's dense or unclear, that's reason enough to slow down.

sections.title: How a fair process actually looks
sections.html:
A fair offer is grounded in your specific deed, acreage, and production history if there is any, explained in terms you can follow, and open to you taking the time you need, including showing it to a Pennsylvania attorney familiar with mineral title if you want a second opinion. There's no reason a legitimate buyer should discourage that.

If you're getting multiple offers, compare the reasoning behind each one as closely as you compare the number itself. The buyer who walks you through their thinking and welcomes your questions is generally a better sign than the one pushing for a fast signature.

sections.title: What our own family learned the hard way
sections.html:
One of the first offers a relative of ours received came with a note claiming it was only good for seventy-two hours, no explanation of how the number was reached, just a signature line and a stamped envelope. She called around, found two other buyers willing to actually look at her deed and statements, and ended up with a far better understanding of what she owned before deciding anything.

That's the pattern worth remembering: a real offer survives you asking questions and taking your time. If a buyer's number falls apart the moment you push back or ask for a second opinion, that tells you something about the offer itself.

faqs.q: Is an unsolicited letter automatically a lowball offer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but a number offered before reviewing your specific paperwork is often a starting point built from general county data rather than your actual interest, so treat it as an opening, not a final figure.

faqs.q: Should you be worried if an offer has a short deadline?
faqs.a: A deadline pushing you to sign within days, especially without time to consult an attorney or compare other offers, is a common pressure tactic worth being cautious about.

faqs.q: What should you ask before accepting any offer?
faqs.a: Ask exactly how the number was calculated, what recent activity in your county it's based on, and whether they've reviewed your deed and production history if applicable. A vague answer is a signal to slow down.

faqs.q: Can you get a second opinion before you sign anything?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a reasonable step for any sale. A Pennsylvania attorney familiar with mineral title, or simply a second buyer's opinion, can confirm whether an offer reflects your actual interest fairly.

faqs.q: What if the offer sounds fair but the paperwork feels rushed?
faqs.a: Slow down anyway. A fair number attached to a rushed process is still worth a second look, especially if the closing documents include language you don't fully understand.

faqs.q: Do lowball offers ever come from operators themselves?
faqs.a: Occasionally an operator or a landman working on their behalf will make a purchase offer alongside lease discussions, and the same scrutiny applies. Ask the same questions about how the number was reached regardless of who's sending it.

image.alt: How to Spot a Lowball Offer mineral rights

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: What actually drives mineral rights value in Pennsylvania, from formation and county activity to lease terms and deductions, without a fake price promise.

sections.html:
Every family wants a number, and every honest answer starts with it depends, which frustrates everyone including us.

We know how unsatisfying it is to ask what your minerals are worth and hear a list of factors instead of a figure. But anyone giving you a firm number before looking at your deed and, if there's production, your royalty statements is skipping steps that actually determine the answer. What we can do here is walk through what genuinely drives value in Pennsylvania, so when a real number does come your way, you understand why it's what it is.

Our own family sat through this same conversation before we sold part of our interest, and the factors below are the ones that actually moved the number, not the ones people assume matter most.

sections.title: Formation, depth, and where you sit in the play
sections.html:
Pennsylvania sits over the Marcellus shale broadly and the deeper Utica in parts of the southwest, and where your acreage falls within those formations matters enormously. Core areas of the northeast Marcellus, counties like Susquehanna, Bradford, and Sullivan, have historically seen some of the strongest well results in the state. Southwest counties like Washington and Greene see activity in both the Marcellus and the deeper, more expensive Utica. Acreage on the flank of the play, or in counties with thinner pay zones, typically sees less operator interest, which affects both lease bonus potential and sale value.

This isn't a judgment on any particular piece of ground, it's simply how operators allocate capital, and it varies with rig count and commodity prices year to year, so activity picture in your county today isn't necessarily where it'll be in five years.

sections.title: Lease status and production history
sections.html:
Unleased acreage with no nearby drilling carries more speculative value than a producing well with two years of clean royalty statements behind it. If you're leased but undrilled, the terms of that lease, royalty fraction, primary term remaining, whether it has a no-deductions clause, all factor into what a buyer will pay, because they're effectively stepping into your shoes under that agreement.

If there's an active well, decline curve and recent monthly volumes matter more than almost anything else, since they let a buyer project future income with some confidence instead of guessing from county averages.

sections.title: Why we won't quote a flat number without your paperwork
sections.html:
Any value talk that isn't tied to your actual deed, acreage, and production varies with activity and commodity prices, and treating it otherwise sets up a number that won't survive a real review of your statements. We'd rather walk through your paperwork and give you a figure grounded in your own situation than throw out a range that sounds good on a landing page and falls apart at the table.

If you're comparing offers, ask each buyer the same question: what specifically in the owner's paperwork led to this number. A real answer references your county's recent activity, your decline curve if you have one, and your lease terms if applicable.

sections.title: A note on the checks we've watched shrink
sections.html:
Our family's own royalty checks looked strong the first couple years after the well came online, then the decline curve did what decline curves do, and post-production deductions took a bigger bite as volumes fell. Watching that happen firsthand is part of why we don't like flat promises about value, because the honest answer changes as the well itself changes.

If you're weighing an offer against years of future royalty checks, ask yourself where your well likely sits on its own decline curve, and how the deductions on your recent statements compare to gross value. That comparison, more than any single number, is what actually tells you whether an offer looks reasonable.

faqs.q: Can you just give you a rough per-acre number over the phone?
faqs.a: We can talk through the factors that drive value in your county, but a specific number depends on reviewing your deed, acreage, and any production or lease paperwork you have. Value varies with activity and isn't something we'll guess at blind.

faqs.q: Are minerals in the core of the Marcellus always worth more?
faqs.a: Typically core areas see more operator interest and stronger well results, which supports higher lease and sale activity, but individual tract factors, lease terms, and deduction levels still matter within any county.

faqs.q: Does unleased acreage have any value if nothing's drilling nearby?
faqs.a: It can, particularly if the formation quality and county activity trend suggest future interest, but it's a more speculative valuation than a producing interest with statements to review.

faqs.q: How do post-production deductions affect what your minerals are worth?
faqs.a: Heavier deductions reduce the net royalty income a buyer can expect from a producing interest, which lowers the value even when gross production is strong, so we always ask to see recent statements.

faqs.q: Do Act 13 impact fees affect what your minerals are worth?
faqs.a: Not directly, since the impact fee is paid by the operator to the county, not deducted from your royalty. It's more useful as context for how active drilling is in your county than as a factor in your own valuation.

image.alt: What Are Mineral Rights Worth? mineral rights

items.name: How Minerals Are Appraised
items.meta: The methods buyers and appraisers actually use to value Pennsylvania mineral rights, from discounted cash flow to comparable sales, explained plainly.

sections.html:
A cousin of ours once got three numbers from three different people for the same acreage, and none of them explained how they got there.

Appraisal sounds like it should be a science, and to a point it is, but the honest truth is that mineral valuation in Pennsylvania blends a few different methods depending on whether your interest is producing, leased and undrilled, or entirely unleased. Anyone quoting you a number without asking which situation you're in is guessing more than appraising.

We've sat across the table enough times to know owners want to understand the mechanics behind a figure, not only be handed one. Here's how it actually gets built, method by method.

sections.title: Discounted cash flow, for producing interests
sections.html:
If your minerals are already producing under a well, the primary method is a discounted cash flow analysis: projecting future royalty income based on the well's decline curve, current and expected gas prices, and the post-production deductions showing up on your actual statements, then discounting those future payments back to a present value because a dollar received five years from now is worth less than one in hand today.

The decline curve matters enormously here. Marcellus and Utica wells typically show a steep initial decline in the first one to three years, then flatten into a longer, lower-volume tail. A buyer using your recent royalty statements can model where your well sits on that curve, which is why several months, ideally a couple years, of statements produce a far more defensible number than a single check.

sections.title: Comparable sales and lease bonus data
sections.html:
For unleased or recently leased acreage without production history, buyers lean more on comparable data: recent lease bonus amounts paid nearby, recent mineral sale prices in the same township or county, and permit activity showing whether operators are actively pursuing that formation in your area. Bradford, Susquehanna, Washington, and Greene counties, for example, have very different activity pictures right now, and a fair valuation reflects that rather than treating all of Pennsylvania the same.

This method is inherently rougher than cash flow analysis because it's inferring value from neighbors rather than your own production, which is part of why unleased acreage tends to carry more valuation uncertainty than a producing well with two years of clean statements behind it.

sections.title: What actually moves the number up or down
sections.html:
Formation and depth matter, since deeper Utica wells cost more to drill than shallower Marcellus wells, affecting operator economics and, in turn, activity pace. Your net mineral acres, your royalty fraction, whether you're in the core of the play or the flank, and how heavy the post-production deductions have been running on your statements all shift the analysis meaningfully.

Be wary of anyone offering a number before reviewing your deed and, if applicable, your production history. A real appraisal, even an informal one for purposes of a purchase offer, starts with your actual paperwork, not a flat rate applied to your county.

sections.title: What we ask for before we talk numbers
sections.html:
When our own family sat down with a buyer, the first thing they asked for wasn't an answer, it was our deed and a stack of royalty statements. That felt backwards at the time, but it made sense once we understood the process: without those documents, any number offered is a guess dressed up as an appraisal.

If a buyer is willing to work through your actual paperwork with you, county activity, decline curve, deduction trend, lease terms if applicable, that's a sign they're building a real number instead of reciting a script. It's a reasonable thing to expect from anyone making you an offer.

faqs.q: Do you need a licensed appraiser to sell?
faqs.a: Not typically for a private sale, though a formal appraisal can be useful for estate or tax purposes. We are a buyer, not a licensed appraiser, so any figure we discuss with you is an offer, not an appraisal for other purposes.

faqs.q: Why did two buyers give you such different numbers?
faqs.a: Different buyers weigh decline curves, deduction trends, and comparable activity differently, and some simply haven't reviewed your actual statements before quoting. Ask each one to walk through their method.

faqs.q: Does unleased acreage get appraised the same way as producing minerals?
faqs.a: No, unleased acreage relies more heavily on comparable lease and sale data nearby since there's no production history yet, which generally makes the valuation less precise than for a producing well.

faqs.q: How much do post-production deductions affect the appraisal?
faqs.a: Meaningfully. Heavier deductions reduce the net cash flow a buyer can expect, which lowers the present value even if gross production looks strong. That's part of why recent royalty statements matter so much.

faqs.q: How far back should your royalty statements go for an appraisal?
faqs.a: A couple years is ideal if you have it, since that gives a buyer enough history to model where your well sits on its decline curve. A single month is better than nothing, but it tells a far less complete story.

image.alt: How Minerals Are Appraised mineral rights

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A step-by-step walkthrough of selling mineral rights in Pennsylvania, from confirming ownership to closing, written by a family that has done it.

sections.html:
We sold a portion of our own family's minerals a few years back, and the owner still remember how few people could explain the process in order.

There's a lot written online about mineral rights values and offers, but not much that just lays out the sequence of what happens, in order, when you actually decide to sell. Our family went through this with a piece of ground in the northern tier, and the process itself wasn't complicated once someone walked us through it. Knowing what happens is what changes it from confusing to manageable.

This is that walkthrough, written the way we wish someone had explained it to us the first time, from figuring out what you actually own through the closing itself.

sections.title: Step one: confirm what you actually own
sections.html:
Before anything else, nail down your net mineral acres and whether your interest is leased, producing, or neither. Pull your deed or the estate documents that established your ownership, and if there's a current lease or an active well, gather recent royalty statements. This sounds basic, but a surprising number of inherited interests in Pennsylvania are held by owners who aren't sure whether their acreage is under lease at all.

If you're not sure, the county recorder of deeds and the register of wills, for inherited interests, are the two places we've always ended up going first. A little digging here saves confusion later.

sections.title: Step two: get more than one look at value
sections.html:
Value for Pennsylvania minerals moves with the play, recent nearby permits, production history if there's a well, and lease terms if it's under one. Get more than a single opinion before you commit; a buyer who wants your interest badly should be willing to explain how they arrived at their number rather than just presenting a figure. Ask what recent activity in your county they're basing it on, and whether they've looked at your actual royalty statements or just county-level averages.

It's fair to be skeptical of any number thrown out before someone has actually reviewed your deed and, if applicable, your production history. Real offers are built from your paperwork, not a formula applied to your acreage alone.

sections.title: Step three: due diligence and closing
sections.html:
Once you agree to move forward, the buyer's title team will examine the county records to confirm your ownership and check for liens, unresolved estates, or conflicting claims. This is where messy inheritance situations tend to surface, and it's normal for it to take a few extra weeks if your title needs clearing rather than something wrong with the deal.

Closing itself is usually a mineral deed, signed and notarized, then recorded at the county courthouse. Funds are typically wired or checked out once the deed is recorded, and from that point the buyer takes over dealing with any operator, lease, or future development on that interest.

sections.title: What happens after you sell
sections.html:
Once the deed records, the buyer typically notifies the operator of the ownership change, if the interest is leased or producing, and requests a new division order in their name. From that point forward, royalty statements, division orders, and any future lease negotiations go to the buyer rather than to you.

Keep your own copy of the closing documents and the recorded deed for your records, even after the sale is complete. It's rare that anything comes up years later, but if it does, having your file organized saves a phone call to the courthouse.

faqs.q: How long does the whole process usually take?
faqs.a: With clean title and straightforward ownership, four to six weeks from offer to closing is common. Estates that never went through formal probate, or interests split across multiple heirs, typically take longer.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell your entire interest?
faqs.a: No, many owners sell a portion and keep the rest, especially if they want to retain some upside while addressing an immediate need. Ask any buyer whether a partial sale is on the table.

faqs.q: What if your minerals aren't leased or producing yet?
faqs.a: You can still sell, though the offer will lean more heavily on your county's recent activity and deed acreage than on production history, since there isn't any yet.

faqs.q: Will you need an attorney at closing?
faqs.a: It's not always required, but for estates, split ownership among heirs, or any title complication, a Pennsylvania attorney familiar with mineral title is worth the cost. Many owners bring one for review even on straightforward sales.

faqs.q: What happens to your royalty checks after closing?
faqs.a: They stop coming to you and start going to the buyer once the deed is recorded and the operator updates its records, which is why it's worth keeping a copy of your last statement for your own tax records before that happens.

faqs.q: What's the biggest thing families get wrong the first time?
faqs.a: Assuming the first number they hear is the only option. Getting more than one perspective on your specific deed and paperwork, rather than a single unsolicited letter, usually leads to a better outcome and a clearer sense of what you actually own.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How mineral deed transfers actually work in Pennsylvania, what the recorder of deeds needs, and how heirship and split ownership complicate the process.

sections.html:
The clerk at the recorder of deeds office knew our family name before we introduced ourselves, mostly from all the years we spent tracing this title.

Transferring mineral rights sounds simple until you're standing at a county courthouse counter trying to explain that the deed on file is in your great-grandfather's name and half the heirs live out of state. We've been through that exact conversation. Pennsylvania's mineral title records go back generations in some counties, and understanding how a transfer actually works, deed to deed, is the difference between a smooth closing and a stalled one.

This guide covers the mechanics: what a mineral deed does, how recording works at the county level, and where heirship most often complicates things.

sections.title: What a mineral deed actually transfers
sections.html:
A mineral deed conveys ownership of the oil, gas, and mineral rights in a described tract, separately from the surface. In Pennsylvania, minerals were split from surface ownership many decades ago on a lot of family land, often when someone sold the farm but kept the minerals, or vice versa, which is why you'll sometimes hear the phrase severed estate. Your deed should describe the tract by metes and bounds or by reference to a prior recorded deed, state your fractional or net mineral acre interest, and specify whether it includes executive rights, the right to sign future leases.

When you sell, a new mineral deed is drafted naming you as grantor and the buyer as grantee, describing the same interest, then signed, notarized, and recorded at the county recorder of deeds where the property sits. Recording is what makes the transfer part of the public chain of title going forward.

sections.title: How heirship complicates the chain
sections.html:
If a mineral interest passed down without formal probate, which happens often on older family land in Pennsylvania, the courthouse record may still show a deceased relative as the owner of record. Before a sale can close cleanly, that has to be resolved, usually through probate if the estate was never opened, or through an heirship affidavit and supporting documents if enough time has passed that formal probate is no longer practical under Pennsylvania law.

When an interest is split among several siblings or cousins, each heir typically needs to sign the deed for their fractional share, or the group needs to agree on how the sale proceeds get divided. This is one of the more common reasons a mineral sale takes longer than expected, and it's worth raising with a buyer early rather than after an offer is already on the table.

sections.title: What happens after recording
sections.html:
Once the new deed is recorded, it becomes part of the public record any future title search will find. If the interest is under an active lease, the buyer typically needs to notify the operator with a copy of the recorded deed so future royalty payments and division orders route to the new owner rather than to you.

Keep a copy of everything for your own records, even after the sale closes. County recording systems are generally reliable in Pennsylvania, but having your own file saves time if any question comes up years later.

sections.title: Executive rights and partial interests worth understanding
sections.html:
Some older Pennsylvania deeds split even further than surface and minerals, separating the executive right to sign leases from the royalty interest itself. If your deed carries unusual language like this, it's worth having it reviewed before you sell, since it affects exactly what you're able to convey to a buyer.

Similarly, if you only own a fractional or partial interest in a larger tract, alongside cousins or other family branches, your deed should describe your specific share clearly. A title examiner can usually trace how that fraction was arrived at, even when the math spans several generations of splits.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a mineral deed and a lease?
faqs.a: A deed transfers ownership permanently. A lease only grants a company the right to explore and produce for a set term in exchange for royalty, while you keep ownership of the minerals themselves.

faqs.q: Do all heirs have to agree to sell?
faqs.a: Generally, yes, each heir's fractional share needs to be conveyed by that heir, or by someone with legal authority to act for them. Some heirs can sell their share while others keep theirs, split by interest.

faqs.q: What if the deed is still in a deceased relative's name?
faqs.a: This is common on older Pennsylvania family land. It usually needs to go through probate, or an heirship affidavit if enough time has passed, before a clean transfer can be recorded.

faqs.q: Does recording a deed cost money?
faqs.a: Yes, Pennsylvania counties charge a recording fee, and depending on the transaction there may be a realty transfer tax consideration, so ask your closing team or CPA how that applies to your specific sale.

faqs.q: What are executive rights and do you have them?
faqs.a: Executive rights are the authority to sign a lease on the minerals; some old deeds separate them from the royalty interest itself. Check your deed language, or have it reviewed, since it changes what you can convey in a sale.

items.name: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: What Pennsylvania mineral owners should know about capital gains, basis, and Act 13 impact fees before selling, plus why we say talk to your CPA once.

sections.html:
Somebody in our family always asks the same question at the closing table: what does this actually cost us come April.

We sold a piece of our own mineral interest years ago, and the sale itself was the easy part. The part that took longer was figuring out what we owed the following spring, and separating that from a different question that kept coming up in conversations with neighbors: what is this impact fee the owner keep hearing about, and is that the same as a tax on the owner's royalty. It isn't, and the two get mixed up constantly in Pennsylvania because Act 13 changed how this state handles unconventional gas revenue in a way most other producing states don't.

This guide covers both pieces, plainly and without pretending to be your accountant. It's meant to help you walk into a conversation with a CPA already knowing the right questions, not to replace that conversation.

sections.title: How a mineral sale is typically taxed
sections.html:
When you sell mineral rights outright, the IRS generally treats it as a sale of real property, which usually means capital gains treatment rather than ordinary income. Whether it's long-term or short-term depends on how long you or the person you inherited from held the interest, and inherited minerals typically get a stepped-up basis to the fair market value at the date of death, which can significantly reduce the taxable gain compared to what an ancestor originally paid or was granted.

Contrast that with royalty income from a lease, which is generally taxed as ordinary income each year you receive a check, with depletion allowances that can offset part of it. A lot of families default to holding and leasing because that's what their parents did, without ever comparing the tax treatment of a sale against years of ordinary-income royalty checks. That comparison is worth having with a CPA before you decide either way.

sections.title: Act 13 impact fees: not a tax on you
sections.html:
Pennsylvania is unusual among major gas-producing states because it doesn't levy a severance tax on unconventional wells. Instead, Act 13, passed in 2012, created an impact fee that unconventional well operators pay annually per well, collected through the Public Utility Commission and distributed to counties and municipalities, with a share going to statewide conservation and infrastructure programs. It's meant to offset road wear, emergency services, and other local costs tied to drilling activity, not to fund the state general budget the way a severance tax would.

The reason we bring this up on a page about your taxes is that owners often assume the impact fee comes out of their royalty, or that it's the same as the severance taxes their cousins in Texas or Oklahoma deal with. It isn't. The impact fee is paid by the operator, not deducted from your check, and it has no direct bearing on your personal capital gains or income tax liability. Where it does matter is context: Act 13 is part of why Pennsylvania's regulatory and county-revenue picture looks different from other basins, and it's worth understanding if you're weighing what your county gets from drilling activity near your land.

sections.title: Basis, records, and what to bring to your CPA
sections.html:
If you inherited your minerals, the single most useful document you can hand your CPA is anything establishing date-of-death value, an estate appraisal, a probate filing, even a documented offer from around that time. Without it, your basis defaults to whatever can be reconstructed, which often understates it and overstates your taxable gain.

If you're comparing a sale offer against continuing to hold and lease, bring recent royalty statements too, so your advisor can weigh the ordinary-income royalty path against a capital-gains sale. Every family's basis and tax bracket situation is different, so talk to your CPA or tax advisor before you sign anything, but at least now you're walking in with the right questions instead of just a number on an offer letter.

faqs.q: Do you pay the Act 13 impact fee out of your royalty check?
faqs.a: No. The impact fee is paid annually by the well operator directly, not deducted from royalty owner payments. It funds county and municipal programs, separate from your personal income or capital gains taxes.

faqs.q: Is selling your mineral rights taxed differently than lease royalty income?
faqs.a: Generally yes. A sale is usually treated as a capital gain on real property, while lease royalty checks are typically ordinary income each year. The better path depends on your basis, tax bracket, and how long you plan to hold, so this is a CPA conversation.

faqs.q: What if you don't know what your ancestor paid for the minerals originally?
faqs.a: If you inherited the interest, your basis is usually the fair market value at the date of death rather than the original purchase price, which is often more favorable. An estate appraisal or probate record helps establish that value.

faqs.q: Does Pennsylvania have a state severance tax on gas production?
faqs.a: No, Pennsylvania uses the Act 13 impact fee model instead of a per-unit severance tax, which is different from states like Texas, Oklahoma, or North Dakota. That's a structural difference worth knowing if you're comparing notes with owners elsewhere.

faqs.q: Should you sell before or after year-end for tax reasons?
faqs.a: Timing can matter depending on your income in a given year and whether you have other gains or losses to offset. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about timing before you commit to a closing date.

items.name: Lease vs. Sell: Which Is Right?
items.meta: How Pennsylvania mineral owners weigh leasing against selling, covering royalty income, deductions, risk, and what changes the decision from family to family.

sections.html:
The owner's uncle leased his piece and never regretted it. The owner's mother sold hers and never looked back either. Both were right for their own situation.

This is the question that comes up at every family gathering once someone finds out there's gas activity near the old home place. Should we lease and wait for royalty checks, or sell and take a number now. There isn't a universal right answer, and anyone who tells you there is hasn't sat with enough families going through it. What we can offer is how the tradeoffs actually play out for Pennsylvania owners, because the two paths carry genuinely different risks and rewards.

We've watched both sides in our own family. It comes down to your tolerance for waiting, your need for cash now, and how many people the interest is split between.

sections.title: What leasing actually gives you
sections.html:
A lease keeps you as the mineral owner and entitles you to royalty payments if and when a well is drilled and produces, plus typically a bonus payment up front for signing. The upside is real: production can run for years, sometimes decades, and you keep the asset for your children. The downside is just as real: there's no guarantee a well ever gets drilled during the lease term, and even if it does, royalty income in Pennsylvania is reduced by post-production deductions, taxed as ordinary income each year, and subject to natural production decline that can shrink checks faster than owners expect.

Leasing also means staying engaged with the paperwork indefinitely, division orders, statements, potential heirship issues down the line if you pass the interest to multiple children who then have to agree on everything together.

sections.title: What selling actually gives you
sections.html:
Selling converts the uncertainty of future production into a known amount today, generally taxed as a capital gain rather than ordinary income, and it removes you from the ongoing relationship with an operator entirely. There's no more waiting on statements, no more wondering whether deductions crept up this quarter, no more managing the interest across heirs after you're gone.

The tradeoff is obvious: you give up any upside if activity increases, prices rise, or a well outperforms expectations. If the interest is unleased and there's no drilling planned nearby, selling also means giving up a lease bonus you might have collected first. It's a real decision, not a formality, and worth weighing against your own finances rather than a general rule.

sections.title: The questions we actually asked ourselves
sections.html:
Do we need the money now, or can we afford to wait years for a well to be drilled and produce, if one ever is. How many people would need to agree on every future decision if we keep the interest, and are we confident that agreement will still be easy in twenty years. How do we feel about post-production deductions eating into a check every month versus a single number we control today.

There's no formula that spits out the right answer. Some of our relatives leased and are glad they held on through the years of statements and deductions. Others sold and were relieved to be done managing paperwork tied to land none of them lived near anymore. Both were reasonable choices for the people who made them.

faqs.q: Can you lease first and sell later?
faqs.a: Yes, and many owners do exactly that, collecting a lease bonus and then selling the leased interest, sometimes at a higher value once there's production history to point to. It depends on whether you're willing to wait.

faqs.q: Is selling always worth less than waiting for royalties?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Royalty income depends on a well actually being drilled, performing well, and holding up against post-production deductions and decline. A sale removes that uncertainty in exchange for a known amount now.

faqs.q: What if your interest is split among several siblings?
faqs.a: Split ownership often pushes families toward selling, since managing decades of shared decisions across multiple heirs and their own children gets harder with each generation. Some siblings sell while others keep their share, which is usually fine to structure.

faqs.q: Does it matter whether there's already a well producing?
faqs.a: It matters a great deal. Producing interests have real statements to evaluate, which usually supports a stronger, better-documented offer than an unleased interest with no production history yet.

faqs.q: How do taxes differ between the two paths?
faqs.a: Royalty income from a lease is generally taxed as ordinary income each year, while a sale is usually treated as a capital gain. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about which path fits your situation before deciding.

faqs.q: What if you only want to sell part of your interest?
faqs.a: Many owners split the difference, selling a portion while keeping the rest under lease. It's worth asking a buyer whether a partial sale is something they'll structure, since not every situation is all or nothing.

faqs.q: Does it matter if you is the only heir versus one of several?
faqs.a: Being a sole owner simplifies either path, since there's no group decision needed. Shared ownership among siblings or cousins often tilts the decision toward selling, simply because coordinating future lease decisions across many heirs gets harder over time.

investing.title: Mineral Investing

items.name: How to Evaluate a Mineral Package

sections.title: Locate the Interest on the Pennsylvania Record
sections.html: A Pennsylvania mineral investment should be traced from the recorded interest through the lease and unit to the paid decimal before a yield or multiple is trusted. The review begins with the source deed, reservation language, acreage, formation and depth limits, lease royalty clause, amendments, unit declaration, tract participation, division order, and payor record. Those documents should describe the same county interest and owner fraction. An investment becomes useful to compare only after the ownership record and the income record can be reconciled, without assuming that a nearby well, a county production total, or one recent check represents the asset being evaluated.

sections.title: Stress the Statement by Production Month
sections.html: Volumes, realized price, products, taxes, gathering, compression, transport, processing, prior-period adjustments, downtime, and suspense releases can move independently and should be tested across several statement months. A sound underwriting model retains the operator, property and well identifiers, production month, sales month, product, gross volume, owner decimal, gross value, each deduction, taxes, net value, and any adjustment code. Comparing those fields across a consistent period exposes whether a change came from production, price, the paid decimal, a deduction category, a correction, or a release from suspense. That is a stronger starting point than annualizing the latest deposit.

sections.title: Write the Downside Case First
sections.html: A disciplined Pennsylvania mineral model tests lower volumes, weaker pricing, wider deductions, longer downtime, title expense, operator concentration, delayed development, and limited resale liquidity before assigning value to upside activity. The written case should distinguish producing value from undeveloped optionality, identify which assumptions come from private records, and label which assumptions rely only on public context. It should also test the cost and timing of curing probate, trust, entity, or fractional-title issues. A buyer or owner can then compare the expected cash flow, downside case, holding period, and sale alternatives without treating uncertain future wells as guaranteed production.

A sound underwriting model retains the operator, property and well identifiers, production month, sales month, product, gross volume, owner decimal, gross value, each deduction, taxes, net value, and any adjustment code. Comparing those fields across a consistent period exposes whether a change came from production, price, the paid decimal, a deduction category, a correction, or a release from suspense. That is a stronger starting point than annualizing the latest deposit.

sections.title: Write the Downside Case First
sections.html: A disciplined Pennsylvania mineral model tests lower volumes, weaker pricing, wider deductions, longer downtime, title expense, operator concentration, delayed development, and limited resale liquidity before assigning value to upside activity. The written case should distinguish producing value from undeveloped optionality, identify which assumptions come from private records, and label which assumptions rely only on public context. It should also test the cost and timing of curing probate, trust, entity, or fractional-title issues. A buyer or owner can then compare the expected cash flow, downside case, holding period, and sale alternatives without treating uncertain future wells as guaranteed production.

sections.title: Locate the Interest on the Pennsylvania Record
sections.html: A Pennsylvania mineral investment should be traced from the recorded interest through the lease and unit to the paid decimal before a yield or multiple is trusted. The review begins with the source deed, reservation language, acreage, formation and depth limits, lease royalty clause, amendments, unit declaration, tract participation, division order, and payor record. Those documents should describe the same county interest and owner fraction. An investment becomes useful to compare only after the ownership record and the income record can be reconciled, without assuming that a nearby well, a county production total, or one recent check represents the asset being evaluated.

exchange-1031.title: Mineral 1031 Exchange Guides

items.name: Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You?

sections.title: Place the Timeline on the Exchange Calendar
sections.html: Potential exchange treatment should be discussed with a qualified intermediary and independent tax counsel before a Pennsylvania mineral sale closes or proceeds are received. The working calendar should show the proposed sale date, intermediary engagement, control of proceeds, identification deadline, acquisition deadline, replacement-property review, lender milestones, title work, and closing dependencies. The Pennsylvania mineral buyer can provide transaction records, but cannot decide tax eligibility or replace the owner’s advisors. Recording who is responsible for each dated step helps prevent a title correction, settlement revision, or late document request from being mistaken for an extension of a federal deadline.

sections.title: Keep Pennsylvania Title Work and Federal Timing Distinct
sections.html: Deed work, probate, heirship, trusts, corrective instruments, payor records, and county recording can move on a different schedule from exchange deadlines. A careful review should identify the current record owner, vesting instrument, legal description, mineral or royalty estate, county, owner fraction, lease and unit references, retained rights, and any unresolved estate or entity authority. Those items determine what can be conveyed and who can sign. The intermediary, tax counsel, title professionals, and transaction parties should receive the same dated description of the asset so a Pennsylvania title cure does not quietly alter the property scope or the exchange paperwork.

sections.title: Match the Property Scope
sections.html: The sale agreement, deed, legal description, retained-rights language, settlement statement, intermediary instructions, and replacement identification should not quietly change the tract, estate, formation, depth, county, owner fraction, or entity. Before closing, the file should compare those descriptions line by line and retain the final signed documents, funding confirmation, intermediary record, and county recording reference. Any boot, debt replacement, related-party question, partial sale, entity mismatch, or change in replacement property belongs with qualified tax and legal advisors before reliance. The goal is a documented handoff in which the Pennsylvania mineral conveyance and the exchange record describe the transaction consistently.
